The book of Job has a not insignificant presence in Augustinian production, associated with his pastoral activity i and polemic 2. There are 390 quotations from it, of which half are represented by verses 1,21; 2.9-10; 7.1; 14, 4-5; 28,28 3. To all of them we must add the work Adnotationes in Iob. The work is one of those that Agustín hesitated about whether to make public or not 4. The positive option was motivated by the fact that it was already owned by the brothers whose interest he could not put obstacles °>. Regarding the Adnotationes, it should be said that it is a work that is both rare and difficult. Rare due to its very composition and origin. Augustine reads the book of Job, makes some glosses in the margin, less at the beginning and more as the reading progressed, and leaves the manuscript at that. Later, at a time unknown to us, some people, also unknown to us, were in charge of putting together these glosses, constituting a separate book. We do not know how far the work of these subjects reached. One might think that it was reduced only to extracting new material from Augustine's annotations, putting the annotated text before it. But it is possible that his contribution was greater. In the reference to the Retractationes Augustine points out that they did so to the extent that they could or wanted to. Above all, the "they wanted" leaves room for conjecture. What is Augustine referring to? Why did they select what seemed appropriate to them based on the interests that moved them to do the work? In that sense it could be explained, although it seems The theme of Job was linked to the catechesis of the Lord's Prayer, to the preaching on the appreciation and good use of wealth, and to the exposition of Le 17:34-35 and Ez 14:14 (cf. very unlikely, the lack of glosses referring to the first chapters 6. Or perhaps because they cut when it seemed right, this being the reason that the annotations do not extend to the entire book of Job, but only to the first 39 chapters? In any case, although Augustine's words indicate that his task was redigere in unum, that is, purely material, on the other hand the fact remains that the Saint hesitates between attributing the work to himself or attributing it to them. It is difficult work. Augustine's warning was not necessary to realize it, but he has gone ahead to indicate that there will be very few people capable of understanding it, and not even they will be able to understand everything. He provides the reasons for his statement, namely: a) In numerous passages the commented words have not been transcribed, so sometimes there is the commentary itself, but not the commented text, b) The brevity of the sentences causes a level of obscurity higher than admissible, so it is necessary to go over many texts that are unintelligible, c) The same copy that Augustine had at his disposal was corrupted, without him being able to correct it. While he acknowledges that it is difficult to read, in the same brief review he considers that it will be tasty (suavis) for those few who manage to understand it. In fact, the glosses are not disconnected from each other, but rather follow a line of thought. Job is not considered secundum historiami, but as the personification of the man of the New Testament, of the Church itself 8, who begins by recognizing his situation as a sinner, this being the key that guides the glosses themselves, by explicit confession of its author (6.7,521). In Augustine's interpretation, Job defends his human justice, that is, according to human criteria, which his friends denied him; but he admits his sin before God, so he cannot consider God's behavior towards him unfair. As the text progresses, Job, without abandoning his

confessing condition, he appears more and more as a man of the Church. Controversial references are not abundant, but they are not absent. At least once he seems to think of the Manichaeans when referring to those who claim that the Scriptures contradict each other. The Donatist controversy is more present. It is enough to consider the references to the universality of the Church -<>, to the presence of the evil ", to the claim to establish here the separation between good and evil 12, to schisms and heresies '3 and to unity 14. But a theme dominates that we can call anti-Pelagian ante litteram. Starting from the fact that God made man eternal (14,538), although once he remembers that he was deprived of said immortality by the robbers (17,545), insists on mortality as a punishment that man brought upon himself for his sin (9,530; 10,532; 15,541; 17,544), specifically, for wanting to trust in himself (6,520); mortality in turn is the origin of other tribulations (10,532; 16,544).

A.-M. La Bonnardiére considers the possibility that Augustine had an incomplete text (Bible, p. l 12). However, once (38,601 [In all the references we make, the first data refers to the chapter of the work of Job, while the second, of three figures, usually in square brackets, to the pages of the CSEL 28 edition, indicated in the present edition]) refers to him secundum historiam. Cf. De civitate Dei 18,47, where Augustine considers the book of Job as historical. Cf. note 6 to the text, where we collect the different formulations that Augustine makes of this personification of Job.

The concept of confessio is one of those that appears most frequently in the Adnotationes in lob. We have counted at least 32 presences of it, both in the substantive form and in the verbal form. The first fact that stands out is the minimal or perhaps non-existent presence of the confessio as praise. We have not detected any case that leaves no room for doubt. The confessio in its meaning of recognition of God, that is, as a profession of faith, has a discreet presence: at least four texts leave no doubt. One refers to the recognition of God (confiten deo) in a generic way; another speaks of the confessio that occurs in baptism, that is, the confession of faith (24,560); a third mentions the Church as confessing, that is, believing in God (24,558), and a fourth refers to the confession of Jesus Christ (38,604). The remaining cases refer to confessio as recognition of one's own sin. In many cases the data appears clear, by explicitly linking the two concepts; the confessio and the peccatum. Here is how it is expressed: -radi peccata confitentium» (2,510);-cumcogituradconfessionem... tolluntenimpeccatum- (6,518); -convertantur et confiteantur deo putredine peccatorum- (6,519); -quae (peccata) alii per poenitentiam confitentur- (7,522); -utilitatem... confessionis... peccatum suum proloqui(19,548); -indignitates humanoe vitae... confitetur» (21,553); -solvitur enim per confessionem poenitentis hominis et gratiam ignoscentis dei- (27,564); -a confitente peccata sua et non superciente de meritis operum- (28,567); -si se homines meminerint confitendo peccata sua- (37,599). In other texts the relationship is not explicitly formulated, but the conceptual context makes it equally clear that it is about the confession of sin.

It is understood that there is a confession of sin when said confession involves uttering words against oneself (10,531), an argument to oneself that is what is proper to confession (13,537); a failure to forgive oneself (13,537) In addition to these cases that leave no room for doubt, it is the logical deduction if it appears as an individual offering (victim) compared to the sacrifice that is offered for all sins and for those of everyone (1,509); if God grants his mercy to those who exercise said confessio (5,516); if the authentic man identifies with the one who practices penance through conversion to God and with the one who exercises confession (6,520-1); if it is equivalent to not forgiving one's own mouth and can only be exercised while there is time (7,523); if the one who confesses is a truthful man (8,526); if the confession is linked to pain for the wound itself (16,542); if he complains about being scolded, even though he already confesses (19.549); if it witnesses the threat of God (39,621). All cases where it is clear that it is about confessiopeccati. Confession does not appear in the text as springing spontaneously from the heart of man, but as the fruit of the work of Christ, as an effective result of the grace of the New Testament (28,567); In short, as a work of God. God acts in man, reaching his interior through the darts of his words that pierce his soul, stimulating confession, to the point that man feels forced (cogi) to do so (6,518). Repeatedly Augustine insists that every man needs God's help in his confession (6,519-521). But also the work of man. There is a subjective element, namely, the consideration of the rottenness of one's own sins and the imminence of death that fills one with panic (6.519; 19.548). It is the other element that forces (coactus) the confession. Only this action of man is caused by the previous action of God: man feels driven to confession, once God has enlightened him internally with his word. Without that light, he would not understand the scope of his own situation or his own sin. On the other hand, what is specific about Christian confession is not the simple recognition, but the painful recognition of one's own wound (16,542). It is necessary to add

But the Retractationes place it at number thirteen of those composed after his episcopal consecration, after the Quaestiones gospelrum and before the De catechizandis rudibus. Sticking to them, we must admit that the Adnotationes in lob were written before 400 or 405 18. This is what A.-M. la Bonnardiére does, who places the work in 399 19; D. de Bruyne 20 and G. Bardy 21, who place it in the same way that man can resist it and prevent it, showing himself as a hard and impenetrable stone to the darts of the words of God (6,519). Confession does not appear as another act within the different religious practices that a man can perform, which can be replaced by another. Confession goes to the root of man's relationship with God, on the one hand, and, on the other, to the root of knowing oneself as a man. To the point that the Saint defines the true man from the confessio. It is the criterion that defines the truthfulness and authenticity of man. The authentic man (verus) is the one who exercises the confessio; through this confessio the truth is realized, and that is why it comes to light (Qn 3,21), and is recognized and proclaimed as it is (6,521). The one who exercises confessio and recognizes his sin is not only the authentic man (verus), who does not deceive himself, but also the truthful man who does not deceive others (6,521). That is why the confessio of one's sins is a way of remembering that one is a man (37,599), it is the manifestation of man's poverty before God (36,591), from which the fear of the Lord will spontaneously arise (37,599) and the plea for help to God himself, which is what also characterizes the authentic man (verus). Latin text The Augustinian work bears witness to numerous Latin texts of the book of Job. The one used by the Saint in the Adnotationes is that of the Héronimian hexaplar translation. We know, through his confession2, that in 403 Augustine preferred it to the other one by Jerome written directly on the Hebrew, but later he corrected it on the Greek text 25. But even these must necessarily feel bothered by not understanding many things, since in numerous passages the commented words have not been transcribed, in such a way that it is known what is being commented on. Although in one text he talks about Job secundum historiam, that is, as a concrete person, he was part of the Church (38,601), in the work he loses that individual face to become a character who surpasses himself, who personifies others. Here his plaintive words do not come from a personal inability to endure the whippings, but rather reflect the pain of the entire human race (6.518). Following the simple order of appearance, here are who he personifies: someone who is characterized, among other things, by not boasting about those who trust in temporal goods (6,520); to the man who accuses himself of his wrongdoings (6,521); to the redeemed man, that is, to the Church of which they speak or would speak to the people (17,545); to those who in moments of persecution prefer to suffer rather than give in to the persecutors or flee (24,558); to the confessing Church (24,558); to the Church united to Christ, its head (29,569); to man, that is, to the people of the New Testament, who desire the days predicted by the Lord (29,570); to the soul that has passed from the old man to the new man (29,570); to the entire Church (38,601); to the only people of God (38,607-8); to the Body of the Lord, which is the Church with people who walk slowly (39,626-627); to the Church (17,545). From this function of meaning, it is easy for Augustine to eliminate from Job's words any touch of personal bitterness for the physical ills he suffers, making them an expression of his pain for his sin.

Quia imminente morte terrentur Confession is not, for Augustine, just another act within the different religious practices that a man can perform; one of many that can be replaced by another with identical effectiveness and meaning. Confession goes to the root of man's relationship with God, on the one hand, and, on the other, to the root of knowing oneself as a man. To the point that the Saint defines the true man from the confessio. It is the criterion that defines the truthfulness and authenticity of man.

He states it repeatedly. The authentic man (verus) is the one who confesses; through this confessio he realizes the truth, and that is why it comes to the light 0n 3,21), and recognizes and proclaims himself as he is (6,521). The one who exercises the confessio and recognizes his sin is not only the authentic man (verus), who does not deceive himself, but also the truthful man (verax) who does not deceive others (6,521). That is why the confession of one's own sins is a way of remembering that one is a man (37,599), it is the manifestation of man's poverty before God (36,591), from which the fear of the Lord will spontaneously arise (37,599) and the supplication for help to God himself, which is what also characterizes the authentic man (verus). On the other hand, confessing Christ reveals what is in the heart of man (38,604).

CHAPTER 7. Is not man's life on earth a test? Here he begins to show us the meaning of the previous words. He presents this test as a kind of stadium where there is a fight and where man wins or is defeated. And his life is like that of a day laborer, waiting for temporal pay, so that those who wait for the fruit of righteousness in the future no longer have life on earth. Or is he like the slave who fears his master and has sought the shadow? This symbolically means Adam's hiding from the face of the Lord and covering himself with shadow-producing leaves that man acquired after abandoning God. Or like the mercenary who waits for the salary of his work. The latter differs from the former in that the former had his temporal goods, while the latter limits himself to desiring them. So I have waited empty months. Already in the shadow, he called temporal goods vain. I have had nights full of pain: in them the light of the night is lost.

Let us not interpret it as carnal prostration. They have sewn a hair shirt over my skin: the most intimate sins that remind him that he was once among the good. And on my eyelids the shadow of death: I want to see, but carnal habit prevents me. May the earth not cover the blood of my flesh: that is, although my prayer is not pure because I long for earthly realities, may a pile of earth not collapse on the bonds of my mortality. This is what he has emphasized with the term blood. In short, that because of earthly appetites I do not see myself buried in the greater calamities of a voluntary sin. This voluntary sin is the natural sin that flows from mortality. May there be no place for my cry, may all the merit of my prayer be blocked. Now, then, my witness is in heaven: it seems to refer to the Lord, since he had not yet come down to earth. And up there is my defender: for his participation in mortality. Compare man with the Lord: may the Lord come so that man may be compared to him as John is to Christ. In this comparison one comes to understand the distance between the perfect man and God made man. As the son of man with respect to his neighbor: as the incarnate Lord with respect to him who had fallen into the hands of robbers. For the numbered years have come to me: because the help of Christ will come to me tione magna (lob 16,15): ne carnalem prostrationem intellegeremus. Nec sit locus clamori meo (lob 16,19): intercludatur meritum orationis meae. Et nunc ecce in caelis est testis tneus: de Domino uidetur dicere, quia nondum in terram descenderat. In quorum diiudicatione intellegitur quid distet inter hominem perfectum et Deum hominem factum.

My spirits collapsed, overwhelmed with work as I am. I ask to be buried, but it is not my turn: for the mortal to be absorbed by life. Don't even let your people recognize you. May your tent be saved again under heaven: for some will be saved again. But let others live in his people: let his people be subject to others. CHAPTER 19. Job's response: You are exhausting me with your speeches: you make me sick, when your task was to comfort me. Know, then, that it is God who has made me this way: before him I can be convicted of sin, but not before men. And he has surrounded me with his trenches: the ditch is near the walls. With this pit he blackmails me into confessing to him. I laugh at the discredit and do not speak: allusion to the usefulness of confession. If he tried to laugh at his sin, but not confess it out loud, he would shout, but no one would hear him. He has settled darkness on my face: he has stopped illuminating my face. This is what happens to those who turn their backs on the light. And he tore the crown from my head: the spiritual dignity that wisdom confers. He has left me broken everywhere and I have left: I had everything and he took it from me, even though I had received the power to contain it all. And he counted me among his enemies: he treated me as if I would harm him if I were equal to him. They have camped around my tent: my heart and my conscience. My brothers went away from me: waiting

moria populi. Et non sit cognoscibilis in populo suo: ad tantam deiectionem ueniat, ut a suis non agnoscatur. Nec resaluetur sub cáelo domus eius: aliqui enim resaluabuntur. to correct me, since they are my brothers, although initially they appreciated my correction very little. And they followed some individuals who advised them very strange things. That is, pernicious. And knowing my name, they have forgotten me: they do not know me because I am changed. The guests of my house and my maids: with whom I exchanged my secrets: the flatterers, who distance themselves from those who confess God. They say they all behave like servants. I called my servant and he did not answer me: an allusion to the body, or also to those who were at his service for his immoralities. He would reproach Job for not having judged rightly, since God cannot be rebuked except through intelligence, in which he surpasses us, since man receives it from him. And will he enter into judgment with you?: that you may compare yourself with him. Your light has turned into darkness: your dignity. Do you want to keep the path of the century?: as if Job thought that God does not care about human vicissitudes. Why were they caught before they were mature?: immature, in their opinion, since they planned to remain here forever, or in any case before accessing wisdom. CHAPTER 35. Why did you think that? Why have you judged like this? Who are you to say: I am righteous in the presence of the Lord? In the presence of the Lord you said: I am righteous. Two things are reprehensible in man: one, to claim both proudly and falsely that one is just, even according to human standards of justice; another: it can never truly be said by a man that he is righteous in the presence of God, in comparison with which any man is wicked. Or do you say: What good is it to you or what am I going to do if I have sinned? CHAPTER 36. Bear with me a little and I will teach you; I still have words left. Taking my knowledge from afar: Because while we are in this body we are pilgrims separated from the Lord. I will speak with my works, which are righteous: so that what God throws in the sinner's face will not be reproached: Who are you to number my commandments and to take my covenant in your mouth? You, who hate discipline? That is why here we must speak with the works: because knowledge is taken from afar, in a fragmentary and enigmatic way. But when what is perfect arrives, what is fragmentary will disappear and then it will no longer be from afar, because we will see it as it is. And you will not take true words as unjust. The same evils that Job suffered are words from God based on truth and just, but he believes that he understands them in an unfair way. He thinks that he complains of suffering without reason, whereas, regarding the tribulation of the righteous, it is said: The time has come when judgment begins at the house of the Lord. And keep in mind that God does not despise the innocent, although he punishes those whom he loves well and scourges everyone whom he welcomes as a son. The strong man by the strength of his heart does not give life to the wicked: even if he seems to forgive him temporarily. It is well qualified: strong because of the vigor of the heart, because it will not quicken it

Have you understood the bonds of the Pleiades or opened the fence of Orion? Or will you open Mazuroth in due time? Or will you drive Vesperus over his building? Will we have to use astronomy and know the characteristics of these stars to be able to interpret the passage? I'm surprised that it fits well within our discourse. Otherwise, the text is quite wordy. To something else, then. After mentioning the names of some stars and taking into account the figure of speech in which the whole is taken for the part, will it be necessary to understand all the stars in them? (If Mazuroth is a star, we do not find its correspondence in Greek, and it seems very clear that it is a Hebrew word.) In the same way the whole is taken for the part in the text: I have begotten you before the star. Because the star was not the first within creation, so that it seems that "before the star" is equivalent to "before every creature", but rather that in the star are represented all the stars, the whole by the part. And by all the stars are understood all times (because it is written of the stars that they serve as signs for the seasons), to refer to the Lord, born before all times, not in time and, therefore, coeternal with the Father. The quote of the

Pleiades, Orion, Mazuroth and Vesperus are made as a compendium of all the stars. If the exclusive quotation of the star enters into the locution of which we have spoken, with how much greater reason does the quotation of the rest of the names of the stars? Why, then, in a text it is said you understood the ties; in another, you opened; in another, opening at its time, and in another, will you drive over its building? They are properties of the stars mentioned in their order. Or could it also be accurately said: “you opened the hedge of the Pleiades” and “you understood the bonds of Orion”? The other two elements can also be exchanged. Let us take as a guideline the passage of the psalm: He who dwells in the heavens will laugh at them; The Lord will mock them. Its meaning would change absolutely nothing if it said: He who dwells in heaven will mock them and the Lord will laugh at them. The Lord is the same. Similarly, both the names of the Pleiades and that of Orion mean the same thing if all the other stars are considered to be included in both. Thus, in the word stars, all those who have citizenship in heaven are included within the bosom of the Church. And by ties we understand the links that they and God have between themselves, links that prevent them from falling. But charity never falls. Because God denied him wisdom and gave him no share in intelligence: is there anything more foolish than trusting in vanities and working to achieve perishable things without fear of losing them? There are many people with this mentality. Those who enjoy long worldly happiness think this way in particular, especially if it enjoys an uninterrupted succession going back to grandparents and great-grandparents. A sudden misfortune does not fit their minds. The comparison of these people with ostriches seems accurate to us because their appearance on earth has characteristics of greatness, but they do not have the wings of virtue nor do they enjoy contact with heaven. However, pay attention to what follows: When the time comes, he will soar into the clouds and laugh at the horse and the rider: After the fullness of the time had come in which the rich of this world were commanded not to be haughty nor to put their trust in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, they began to lift up their hearts toward the Lord and laugh at the proud persecutors whom the Lord cast into the sea. a martyr, a fearless and joyful witness of saving faith, but not by his own power, but by that granted to him by the Lord. Have you endowed his throat with neighing? Put on the armor of God to be able to withstand the day of trouble. And of the boldness of the glory of his chest? This is the boldness that Isaiah boasts about and that makes him talk; The glory of the breast is the conscience that purifies the works of man so that each one has the glory in himself and not in another. When he goes out into the field, he frolics: when he comes out into the light of freedom, he leaps for joy at the ease of good works performed within the ease of charity. He bravely goes out to war: against the temptations of setbacks. He goes out to meet the darts, despising them: because he lives close to his weapons, among which he has the shield of faith, against which the incendiary darts of the enemy are blunted. And he does not shrink from the sword: it can refer to visible death. It can also be an allusion to those with refractory sensitivity to the truth or to those who are subtle in their sectarian attitude. He is not intimidated by them, because he is also encouraged to love them. The bow and the sword dance with joy over him: through personal confession the threat of God who announces invisible punishments in the distance is ratified. It also champions the testimony of the word that in a certain way destroys all errors closely. Of course it is one thing to threaten the future.

of this type he meets those who are already dead to this world, given the feelings with which they renounce the devil, he has no hesitation in offering them the oral ministry translated into words, and with them he brings them highly qualified to the body of the Church. That is why he continues: And where there is carrion, there they will be immediately. The Lord answered and said. From the fact that the Lord now repeats his speech, despite the fact that he had the floor, it is understood that Job fell silent, stupefied, upon hearing such things, and did not dare to speak more. In the next two verses there is an invitation from the Lord for Job to answer him. Can he who argues with the Almighty remain silent? That is, why are you silent, if you are arguing with the Almighty? Can he who tries to reply to God respond like this? Converting the phrase completely into an interrogative style, it becomes like this: Does he who responds like this in his discussion with God reply to God? Arguing with the Almighty in this passage has a nuance of searching, not of replying. Not because He is Almighty are we going to stop arguing with Him. Because to argue with God, nothing that comes from Him in the course of a reasoned dispute is not required as a prerequisite, as if it emanated from the truth itself. There is another interpretation. It could be this: does he who argues with the Lord rest? That is to say, since he who argues with the Almighty does not rest, one does not have to argue with Him to rest. The one who argues usually wears the

contrary, and he who is contrary to God cannot rest, that is, he does not find rest, unless he conforms without the slightest contradiction to the will of God. Therefore, when replying to God he will respond like this, that is: when in the discussion he responds to God, he replies to God and that is why he finds no rest. Hence the expression: O man! Who are you to reply to God? But we wonder: did Job ever do this? Well, God does not consider him as his competitor or opponent, which is what his friends who understood nothing did. Such is the testimony that appears at the beginning and at the end of the book. Wouldn't Job have expressed himself like this to personify the body of the Lord which is the Church, where there is a very important sector of weak people, not desperate cases, but those who are even in danger regarding their personal benefit, whose feet I am about to say barely move and whose steps advance even less because they envy sinners and seeing the peace they enjoy? They are the same ones who say: Does God know? Does the Almighty know him? There you have it: the same sinners and the rich of the world obtained riches. Have I kept my heart clean in vain, have I washed my hands among the innocent, have I done nothing but receive whippings and see myself punished every morning? INTRODUCTION In 1958 P. Rollero wrote: «The De consensu evangelistarum is the most important work of Augustine in the first years of his episcopal activity and the best among his exegetical works» i. Several decades later we have great difficulty in agreeing with such a statement. The new exegetical methods to which, in the Catholic sphere, Vatican II gave a letter of legality and the results obtained modify the evaluative judgment on the method and achievements of Augustinian exegesis and, consequently, on De consensu. But in no way does it imply that the work has to be relegated to absolute oblivion. This would mean a lack of historical sense and an enormous act of injustice. Several aspects deserve recognition: the great effort he made, in the service of a noble cause, at a time when he was overwhelmed by other work, and with the only methodology capable at that time of providing positive results. The great effort is understood if we take into account that he lacked our good evangelical synopses. If some are capable of being surprised that he did not perceive all the variants of one text with reference to another, others are even more surprised that he has reached the level he did in this regard. Without forgetting that the argument e silentio must be used with great caution. The work is not by the scholar Augustine, but by the pastor Augustine. For now, its origin must be seen in a request from the brothers who, "keeping their faith intact, want to know what they can answer to the questions... either to advance in their own science, or to refute their talk" (1,7,10). That is why Augustine undertakes the task of demonstrating the error or recklessness of those who believe they present sufficiently sharp objections against the four books of the Gospel (i b). In fact, anyone who considers it as an investigation into harmony between sacred authors would misunderstand Augustinian writing. Date of composition The authors do not agree on the date of composition of De consensu. The temporal margin in which they all move goes from 400 to 415. F. Weihrich, the Viennese editor of the work, places his composition at the end of 399 21, who is followed by H. Vogels 22, who expands the framework of possibilities until the first part of 400. In the same 400 they place it, in addition to the Maurinos", R. A. Markus 24, S. Zarb 25, J. Lamotte 26 and G. Bardy 2?. The reasons that support these positions are summarized in the following: Augustine's information in the Retractationes that he composed it once he had begun the De Trinitate; the probable allusion to the laws of Honorius in 399 against the pagans; the points of contact with the Contra Faustum and with the Quaestiones gospelrum, and the possible reference to De consensu in Epistula 71,4,6 to Jerome in which he speaks of the Vulgate, which he would have used to compose the work. Structure The work, of notable breadth, has a very clearly defined structure. The first book is of a general nature, the remaining three are concerned with showing the falsity of the accusations leveled against the evangelists, in the sense that they contradict themselves or others. The first begins by affirming the authority of the evangelists and their foundations (1,1-2,3); then he deals with the peculiar traits of each one (2,4-6,9), to conclude with the reason for writing the work, that is, to show the harmony between them (7,10-35,54). But in the middle of this last section he introduces a long parenthesis (7:11-34:52) against those who honor Christ as a wise man, and therefore do not want to believe the gospels, as not written by him, but by his disciples, who falsely attributed divinity to him. The first dealt with the rules, the theoretical study of the language and its laws, the "technical" analysis of the sentence and its parts; while the second, of the aspects related to the content and formal beauty, and specifically the commentary of the text. It is this second one that concerns us. In our work the traces of the different moments are perceived: that of the lectio (correct inflection of the voice), that of the emendatio (recourse to the codices) and above all that of the explanatio. As an explanator it provides essential data about each author <•<>, discovers his general intent or particular voluntas'i; characterizes the writing and the material that composes it; examines the words in their morphology, in their meaning, whether proper or figurative, and in their virtutes: latinitas, perspicuitas and ornatus; He does the same with the tocutions, analyzing the syntactic data, their own or figurative meaning and their virtutes; examines the dispositio of the material, in particular the ordo narrationis, with the figures that give reason for the departure from the ordo rerum and, finally, the virtutes narrationis. The first moment, we said, was constituted by lectio; It included separating words, members and periods, and marking, through silences and voice inflections, everything that today our complex punctuation system is responsible for indicating 52. With a different voice inflection you can change the meaning of a text. The tone of voice can give affirmative or doubtful meaning, approval or disapproval, to any sentence, and from there eliminate a difficulty. Next to the lectio was the emendatio. In a world in which the printing press had not standardized the texts and variants were frequent, the comparison and evaluation of the different codices was imposed to opt for one reading in preference to another. In De consensu we notice how Augustine considers their number, their antiquity, their language, their mendacity, and their official status on numerous occasions. But it is necessary to add that such recourse to the codices does not properly serve the emendatio, but rather the explanatio. In fact, Augustine's procedure does not consist in preferring one reading to another, but in giving an explanation of one and the other. He considers them as alternative readings, but not exclusive of each other 53. Although traces of the praxis of lectio and even of emendatio are perceived in De consensu, the work is above all an explanatio of the evangelical texts considered as a whole. Augustine begins with a general assessment of the evangelists. Already in the frontispiece of the work, but not only there, the Saint presents each one of them, marking the particular features that define them and their mutual relationships (1,2,4; 1,6,9; 2,66,127; 2,80,157; ​​4,10,11). As if to justify taking care of them, he ponders his authority. To enable the understanding of their respective writings, it presents the general intention that motivated them. And from here, the comparative "commentary" that aims to deny its inconvenience and demonstrate its consistency^4. Every gospel is a narratio and the evangelist is a narrator. As such, he establishes his own dispositio of the material, his own ordo narrationis, sometimes following the ordo rerum and other times the ordo recollectionis, which must be attributed partly to God, who regulates and governs his memories, and partly to his free decision and literary tastes 56. But they do not seem sufficient to prove the truth and harmony of the different gospels, since the fact persists, noted by every reader, of the notable differences between the different stories. Other more specific arguments are required to demonstrate that the difference does not imply incoherence or contradiction. And Augustine contributes them, not from philosophies or theologies, but from the simple consideration of a literary critic of said writings. He warns that theological objections are supported by others of a literary nature. There is an underlying criticism which is the incoherence and internal and external contradiction of the stories (discrepare sibi et inter se), which deprives them of all credibility. To affirm this denied credibility, Agustín approaches the texts with the eyes of a literary critic. The immediate objective is to see if that incoherence and contradiction that is attributed to them actually exists. We can simplify Augustine's thesis in this way: The accusation of internal incoherence or contradiction among themselves, directed against the evangelists, is the result of ignorance (inerudite: 2,30,76). In fact, where some find difficulty, it can be solved with a lectio that gives the appropriate inflection of voice. It is the resource used to harmonize Mt 14,2 and Le 9,9 (2,43,91), as well as Mt 26,45 and 46 together with Me 14,41 and 42 (3,4,11). He could have taken advantage of the variants between the codices, with the consequent error in one or more of them, to harmonize divergences, but, without opposing others doing so, he preferred not to do so, out of respect for his own principles of textual criticism (3,7,19). Agustín did not lack resources to show that such divergences do not exist, from the very principles of literary criticism. First of all, the breadth of the narratio

Often the difficulties are only apparent, the result of following a different order; One can capture the real order, and another the order of their memories. It is not, therefore, that one evangelist contradicts another, but only that for transcendent reasons or personal freedom they place the narrative material at different moments 76. Evangelical authors make continuous use of the figures of anticipatio and recapitulatio ~n. Now, simply placing something in one place or another in no way affects the truth. Only those who do not realize what it is about can think that the evangelists narrate the same thing contradictorily. Whoever knows the virtues of narratio should not be surprised by the divergences either, knowing that one author, for literary reasons, can opt for a narratio brevis, while another can do so for the narratio aperta, and this will necessarily affect the external form, in that the first can delete or abbreviate narrative elements, and the second can introduce or expand them for greater clarity 78. John, on the other hand, focuses his gaze especially on the very divinity of the Lord by which he is equal to the Father *>. Thus he rises far above the other three - these are seen living in some way with Christ the man on earth; that one, on the other hand, is seen to have transcended the cloud that covers the entire earth, and has reached the clear sky." Or else angels were sent to those prophets who showed them figuratively, through an adequate vision of sensible realities, that the God who created everything was the only true God, to whom everything is subject, and indicated to them how he commanded that they worship him. Augustine's work will consist less of a tractare than of a considerare. In effect, the Augustinian work is not exegetical, it is not a commentary, a tractatio, but a consideratio, which is a prior and distinct intellectual activity. Theconsiderare indicates only the fixation of attention on something, regardless of the activity that follows that activity. Augustine treats the Gospel of Mark as a discourse with its exordium, which adheres to school norms. One of the ways to achieve this is to briefly and clearly show the core of your speech. Matthew, assuming (presenting) Christ as a king who came to this world and to this earthly and mortal life of men to govern us in the troubles of trials, began with Abraham and listed forty people 34. Christ came in the flesh from the same people of the Hebrews, whom God distinguished from the others - and for that purpose he took Abraham out of his land and from his kindred; Thus the announcement of the people from whom he was going to be born contributed to making his prophecy and announcement clearer. By distributing the forty generations into three groups and affirming that from Abraham to David there were fourteen, from David to the transmigration to Babylon another fourteen and another fourteen until the birth of Christ, he did not add up and conclude: all together they make forty-two. In fact, one of the progenitors is counted twice, that is, Jeconiah, with whom the change of direction towards the Gentiles takes place at the time of the transmigration to Babylon. Where the line twists and, to take another direction, forms a kind of angle, the one who makes the angle is counted twice: at the end of the first section of the line and at the beginning. Opposition can be seen, therefore, in one place saying what the other does not say, or another mentioning what the first overlooks56. But the question arises: when could what Matthew combines take place about the march to Egypt and his return from there after the death of Herod, to finally live in the city of Nazareth, where Luke mentions that they returned after they had fulfilled in the temple everything prescribed by the law of the Lord regarding the child? Here, therefore, we must warn something that will later be valid for similar cases, in order to prevent them from disturbing and disturbing the soul in the same way. For example, each evangelist composes his story in such a way that it seems like a sequence that omits nothing; which, by keeping silent about what it does not want to say, adds to the above what it does want, giving the impression of a continuous story '7. But when one relates what the other left out, careful consideration of the order followed allows one to guess the place where the person who overlooked it could have omitted it, to join to the previous thing what he intended to say, as if it were the natural continuation, without interspersing anything'9. Therefore it is understood that where it says that the wise men were warned in a dream not to pass by Herod's house, and that they returned by another way to their uideri potest, quod uel hic dicit, quae ille praetermittit uel ille commemorat quae iste non dicit. In fact, it is known that a second Herod was the son of the first, just like Archelaus, whom Matthew mentions as his successor, upon the death of his father, in the kingdom of Judea; just like Philip, whom Luke mentions as the brother of the tetrarch Herod and in turn tetrarch of Ituraea. A Herod was the king who sought the life of Christ, still a child; The other Herod, his son, was not called king, but tetrarch, a Greek term indicating that he was placed in charge of a quarter of the kingdom. Nam et Mattheus dixit: inuenit hominem sedentem in teloneo (Mt 9,9), nec dixit 'inuenit me', et Iohannes: hic est, inquit, discipulus, qui testimonium perhibet de his et scripsit haec et scimus quia uerum est testimonium The task of the grammaticus was to find out whether a statement is part of the narrative material or introduces it the author on his own account (expersona sua), since sometimes there is a double possibility (ambigue). This situation is perceived here by Augustine and, as a grammarian, he tries to resolve it. Such activity was part of lectio. That is, what causes difficulty is only a locutio (talking about oneself in the third person). The function of the grammatical commentator is to determine the real subject, above the grammatical subject. Although it uses the third person (grammatical subject), the real subject is the first. This is a locutio that Augustine proves to be frequent in Scripture, giving several examples (Mt 9,9; Jn 21,24; Mt 9,6; 16,27; 17,9; Mark 8,31,38; Jn 5,25; Luke 24,46). That is, Augustine comments on the text from the text. Those who see difficulties are because they have not understood it at the grammatical level.

Note that Augustine uses the generic term locutions instead of other more specific ones, undoubtedly for the benefit of the most humble and less cultured. He prefers popular language, understandable to everyone, over scholarly language. In fact, not only do we usually say that something came closer, even before arriving at the place where it is said to have approached - which is why we also say "it came a little closer" or - it came very close -, but we also say that someone has arrived - and with a view to that they came closer -, even if the person who has arrived does not see the person they have reached. This is the case when through a friend you reach someone whose favors you need. The custom in this regard is such that those who reach, with the art of flattery and through appropriate intermediaries, some practically inaccessible powerful people are now vulgarly called perventors (those who arrive). If, then, it is usually said that the same reaching is carried out through other people, how much more reason can it be stated that approaching is carried out through others, which most of the time falls short of reaching, if someone who could not reach, could certainly approach! Thus, without any absurd ies, Matthew meant, also in a condensed form '66, a centurion approached him, which can be vulgarly understood as the centurion approaching the Lord through other people. 50. Father. Abba, in Hebrew, is equivalent to father. Perhaps the Lord used the two terms in response to some mystery, wanting to show that he assumed that sadness on behalf of his body, that is, of the Church, of which he became the cornerstone, reaching him a part of the Hebrews, to which the abba alludes, and another of the Gentiles, to which the father refers*4. The apostle Paul also, not overlooking this mystery, said: In which we exclaim: Abba, Father; and again: God has sent into our hearts his Spirit that cries: Abba, Father! It was appropriate that the good Teacher and true Savior, feeling compassion for the weakest, made it clear in his own person that his martyrs should not lose hope if by chance sadness crept into their hearts at the moment of the passion, as a consequence of human fragility, even though they had overcome it by putting the will of God before their will, since he knows what is best for those for whom he looks out. This is not the best occasion to speak in more detail about all this, since what we are dealing with now is the concord between the evangelists 35. Matthew begins it like this: Then the governor's soldiers took Jesus to the praetorium and gathered the entire cohort around him, they stripped him naked and covered him with a scarlet mantle and, plaiting a crown of thorns, they put it on his head, and in his right hand a reed. It is understood, therefore, that the words of Matthew: They covered him with a scarlet cloak, correspond to those of Mark: They clothed him in purple. If, then, he was handed over to the Jews to be crucified almost at the sixth hour, when Pilate was sitting at the judgment seat, how was he crucified at the third hour? This is what some who did not understand the words of Mark 86 thought. Let's first see what time he could have been crucified; Then we will see why Mark said he had been crucified at the third hour. It was almost the sixth hour when Pilate, sitting on the judgment seat, was said to have handed him over to be crucified. The sixth hour had not already passed, but it was almost the sixth hour; That is, the fifth hour had already passed and the sixth hour had already entered. They would never say -fifth and a quarter' or -fifth and a third' or 'fifth and a half' or anything like that. The Scriptures follow the custom of putting the whole in the »T, especially in the marking of time. This is what happens with those eight days, after which, they say, he went up the mountain. In this regard, Matthew and Mark, counting only those in the middle, said: After six days. Especially considering how restrained John expressed himself by not saying "the sixth hour," but almost the sixth hour. Because, if he had not expressed himself in this way, but had limited himself to indicating the sixth hour, he could say to the pontiffs: non habemus regem nisi Caesarem. Luke's story continues like this: And still without believing it, and full of admiration for the joy, he said -. Do you have anything to eat here? They offered him a piece of roasted fish and a honeycomb. And eating it before them, he gave them the rest. To these words we can add what Luke silences, but John brings up: The disciples were glad to see the Lord. He said to them again: Peace be with you. As the Father has sent me, I send you also. After saying this, he breathed on them and said to them: Receive my Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they will be forgiven, and whose sins you retain, they will be retained. To this we add in turn what John silenced and Luke mentions: And he said to them: These are the words that I spoke to you while I was still with you: Everything must be fulfilled that is written about me in the law of Moses, in the prophets and in the psalms. Then he opened their minds so that they could understand the Scriptures, and he said to them: Thus it is written and thus it was fitting that Christ should suffer and rise from the dead on the third day and that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name in all people.

See how Luke also mentioned the promise of the Holy Spirit, which we only find made by the Lord in the gospel of John. It is not necessary to notice it only in passing, to remember how the evangelists support each other with their testimonies about some things that they themselves do not say, but that they know were said 153. After this, Luke ignores, without the slightest mention, everything that happened, except for the ascension of Jesus to heaven. However, he puts it together as if the event had followed the words spoken, despite the fact that it took place on the first day of the week, the day on which the Lord was resurrected, while the other forty days later, as Luke himself relates in the Acts of the Apostles. John says that the apostle Thomas was not with them then, even though, according to Luke, when those two returned to Jerusalem, one of whom was Cleopas, they found the eleven and those who were with them gathered together. Without a doubt it must be understood that Thomas left there before the Lord appeared to those who spoke these things.

Eccl. 3, 24, 6), Epiphanius (Panarion 51, 5, 3), John Chrysostom {Homilies on Matthew 1,3), that he wrote his gospel in Hebrew, but three times he is equally cautious, preceding the news of a perhibetur, as putting it on account of the others (1, 2, 4; 2, 66, 128; 2, 80, 157; on this aspect of the tradition, denying its veracity and offering another interpretation, cf. J. KÜRZINGER, Papias von Hierapolis und die Evangelien des Neuen Testaments [Regensburg 1983]). In opposition to John, who usually flies on high, Matthew, like Mark and Luke, walks on the earth (4, 10, 15; In lo. ev. 36, 5). In the traditional symbology to which he refers, and which arose in the shadow of Rev 4,7;5,6 and in line with the above, he sides with those who considered that the figure of a lion suited Matthew better (Commentarium in Matthaeum: CC 77, 3, 59-68) than that of a man, even if it meant opposing his teacher Saint Ambrose (cf. Expositio evangelii, prol. 7; also Irenaeus, Adversus Haereses 3, 11, 8).

The reason given is the following: to make the attribution it is not necessary to look at the beginning of the respective books, but rather at the author's overall intent. Now, the lion harmonizes perfectly with Matthew's intention. Matthew is the only one who narrates the coming of the wise men to worship a king; On the other hand, the lion is associated with the royal tribe in the Apocalypse (5, 5), which conforms to the general intention of Matthew (1, 6, 9; 4, 10, 11; In lo. ev. 36, 5). The intention that dominates the gospel of Matthew is to show the royal lineage in the incarnation of the Lord and the conformity of most of what he said and did with the present life of men (1, 2, 4). He proposed to show the royal function of Christ, just as Luke did the priestly one (2, 4, 8; In lo. ev. 36, 5). In fact, like Mark and Luke, he focused primarily on the humanity of Jesus Christ (4, 10, 11). And as a correct writer he adjusted his narratio to this main objective. In this context he also interprets the literary relations he has with Mark, who is supedisequus et breviator (1, 2, 4; 1,3,6). Your

In line with this he attributes the eagle to him. He did not limit himself to writing about the deeds and sayings of the Lord; He also dealt with what the apostles did and said. Furthermore, he was the only one among many whose writing on the matter deserved to be approved by the Church (4,8,9). He wrote in Greek (1,2,4). In contrast to John, who usually flies on high, Luke, like Matthew and Mark, walks on the earth (4,10,15). Luke, like Mark, was not an apostle nor did he follow the Lord in his earthly life. Augustine does not collect any of the data provided by tradition: neither that he was a doctor (Fragmentum Muratonianum), nor that he was one of the 72 disciples who distanced themselves from Jesus after the words about the Eucharist (Jn 6,53) (EPIPHANIO, Panarion 51,11,6), and was recovered by Paul, of whom he became a disciple (IRENEUS, Adversus Haereses 3,1,1; Fragm. Mural.; TERTULIAN, Adversus Marcionem 4,2; EUSEBLO OF CAESÁREA, Hist. 3,24,15; EPIPHANIO, Panarion 51,11,6; Fact that he was obviously not interested in highlighting in this writing because Paul had not been an eyewitness to the deeds and sayings of Jesus either. However, he is interested, for the same reason, in showing his connection with the apostles. He transmits in his gospel what he discovered fideliter in them (1,1,2; Sermo 239,1,1). His task was not purely material in the sense of collecting everything he found; His responsibility was to choose judiciously, from the abundance of material at his disposal, what seemed to him - suitable and consistent - and sufficient for his objective, or, more specifically, what he believed was sufficient to build the faith of the readers or listeners (4,8,9). Although he was not an eyewitness to the events he narrates, his writings could have been approved by the apostles, even while he was alive when he wrote them (4,8,9). If Matthew had Mark as his companion and follower, Luke has no one, a fact that he explains in the following way: the high priest entered the sanctuary alone (1,3,6). That is, this information is in line with the general intention of the evangelist. Luke, in fact, focused his attention (habuisset intentionem) on the priestly function of Christ (1,6,9; In lo. ev. 36,5).

The fact is especially clear in the narration of the genealogy of the Lord, where it reaches David through a non-royal line: through Nathan, contrary to Matthew, who passes through Solomon (1,2,4). Along the same lines, the traditional symbology is placed, which represents him with the image of the calf, and which refers to the sacrificial function of the priests (1,6,9; cf. In lo. ev. 36,5). In fact, along with Matthew and Mark, he dealt above all with the humanity of Jesus (4,10,11). The quality that Augustine highlights in Luke at a literary level is that of clarity. Just as Mark's is primarily a narratio brevis, Luke's is a particularly aperta narratio. On the one hand, it is careful to avoid ambiguous terms (2,3,7); On the other hand, what others leave in the dark he is responsible for clarifying (aperire), both with reference to facts, specifically their manner (2,20,50), or when

(2,35,82), to the place (3,4,13), as to sententiae (2,27,63; 2,77,151; 3,4,13; 3,8,34). Cf. supplementary note 22: 'Narratio brevis et aperta'. The aperire is not the only term that expresses this characteristic of Lucas. Along with him are others that denote the same desire for clarity: illustrare (2,77,151; quae ab istis obscure posita est, inlustrasse sententiam); I will expose (2,5,14); declare (3,18,55: quid ipsa voce magna dixerit declaravit); explicare (3,25,73: praetermisisse Marcum quae Lucas declaravit). Concern for clarity that Augustine points out through adverbs in a comparative degree such as significantius (2,6,9; significantius ipsa tempora expressit), expressius (2,25,57: ad sententiam domini expressius insinuandam), evidentius (2,27,62: evidentius expressit), planius (3,4,13: hoc ipsum planius intimavit) or latius (2,42,90: rem gestam latius indicat). Concern in which in some cases Marcos joins him (2,68,132). Still, only in comparison with Matthew and Mark can we say that Luke is not concerned with brevity. This is a trait that characterizes all evangelists in comparison to the facts themselves. The progression from more to less among the different evangelists is established in this way: Mark is the briefest; then comes Mateo; then Luke; finally John, who, despite being longer than the others, is always brief taking into account the facts themselves (3,13,47). On the other hand, it is due to this desire for brevity that the answers of Philip and Andrew are based on one (2,46,96). Another literary feature of Luke that Augustine highlights is the beauty of form. To the gift of clarity we must add elegance, although the statement is not general (2,27,63: elegant aperuit). Like Matthew, he has enough verborum copy to express elegantly through the verborum differentia his personal narrative purpose (quid singuli suscepissent) (2,3,7). As for the ordo, Luke frequently resorts to recapitulatio and especially to praeoecupatio, which is habitual praxis in him (3,1,2; cf. complementary notes 6: 'Ordo* and 23: 'Praeoecupatio-Recapitulatio-). [5] The number of the gospels. Christian authors of antiquity wondered why there was a fourfold number of gospels. None of them considered it a purely circumstantial fact; rather, they tried to find an explanation, a reference or a meaning. The data is constituted in Origen as a sign of identity for the Church.

He distinguishes the Church from heresy based on the number of gospels it admits. While the latter has many, which he claims to know and have read, the Church only has four, the canonical ones (probata) and the only ones that are to be accepted (Homilies on Luke 1). In the Commentary on John he expresses his opinion that the four gospels are also the fundamental elements of the faith of the Church, and he relates them to the four elements of which the world reconciled with God through Christ is composed (1,4,21). And before him, Irenaeus, while speaking of a single four-dimensional gospel, animated by the same Spirit, affirmed that the gospels are neither more nor less than the four known ones, explaining

candolo in the following way: -Because there are four regions of the world and four main winds; and since the Church is spread throughout the earth and the foundation of the Church is the gospel and the Spirit of life, therefore there are four pillars that breathe incorruptibility from all parts and give life to men" (Adversus Haereses 3,11,8-9). Other authors, both from the East and the West, prefer a more biblical reference: the four rivers of paradise (HIPPOLITUS, Commentary on Daniel
1.17; CYPRIAN, Epistula
73, 10; VICTORINO DE PETTAU, Co-

commentary on the Apocalypse: CSEL 49, 1916, p. 54). Also in the Latin sphere, the author known as Ambrosiáster, in the Líber quaestionum Veteris et Novi Testamenti, expressly raises the question of why the acts and sayings of the Lord are found in four books and have been written by four authors. He responds to this by stating that it was appropriate that the appropriate year of the Lord be contained in four volumes as if they were four turns. In fact, as the year unfolds in four seasons, so that each one needs the other, so the acts and sayings of the Lord are contained in four books that need each other, being perfect only in the fullness of all. He sees the reason for the four authors in that, as the four seasons have different names, that is how the gospels must have had them. From the fact he also extracts an explanation in favor of concord, although it seems that this is not the case (Appendix quaestionum Novi Testamenti 3) • Augustine places himself in this tradition. He also speaks of the gospel quaternarius (S. 95, 3). As for the others, the fact is not without significance; If God wanted it that way, it must be admitted that the fact responds to a significant will. If there are four gospels, it is due, according to him, to the fact that there are four parts of the world where the Church was going to spread, already expressing its universality with that number (1, 2, 6). In fact, it has an ecclesiological value, since the Church is constituted on the four gospels (S. 95, 2. 3). In another place he associates it with the coins found in the fish's mouth, according to Mt 17:23-26: »In his mouth we found two didachmas, that is, four drachmas, because in his mouth we found four gospels. By these four drachmas we are exempt from the tribute of this world, because by the four gospels we will not cease to be debtors, since in them our sins are annulled- (Inpsalmum 137,16). [6] -Ordo-. The ordo is the practical translation of the dispositio. It is at the service of clarity and also ornatus. Classical manuals distinguish between an ordo naturalis and an ordo artificiosus (cf. H. LAUSBERG, Manual, 443-452). The ordo is, without a doubt, one of the most used concepts in Augustinian work. The ordo creates some problems for him and the ordo helps him solve others.

It is evident that the evangelists do not all present the same succession of events. For some, the fact takes away their credibility, since both locations in space and time cannot be true. For Augustine, on the other hand, starting from the diverse ordo to deny the veracity of the gospels is meaningless, precisely because the ordo can be motivated by different factors. And so, what for others is a source of problems, for him will be a source of solutions. Of

In fact, the consideration of the ordo constitutes a key element in the development of the work (2, 5, 16). For now, Augustine recognizes that each author has his own ordo narrandi (1, 2, 4). But it is immediately obvious that this order does not depend exclusively on the author himself. To the extent that it depends on memory itself, and to the extent that it is governed by God with a view to precise objectives, the ordo depends on God (2, 21, 51). Indeed, the succession of memories in the mind of the evangelist is not the result of chance, but the result of the power of God, who regulates them in that specific way with a view to the ordo narrationis (cf. complementary note 15: Memory). In that sense, the criticism of the ordo followed by the evangelists is a criticism of God, and the result of ignorance of the intention of God himself (3, 13, 48). But this is only a part, since Augustine assigns his proper role to the personality of the author. In one text he explicitly states that the evangelist judged that he should put something in the specific place where divine inspiration had suggested it. The iudicatio of the sacred author is linked to the suggestio of divine inspiration (3, 13, 48; cf. 3, 5, 17). He affirms the same thing by indicating that God allowed each author to establish his own order for his narration, leaving it to the investigation of each one to find out the reasons (2, 21, 52). The evangelist is, therefore, responsible for his own order, because even when he faithfully follows the order of his memories, because he knows that they are regulated by God, he does so with complete freedom (2, 21, 51). By stating that the sacred author presents an order as he could and wanted, he is showing the two agents of it: God and himself (2, 21, 52). In the work at hand, Augustine speaks of several orders. He occasionally mentions the ordo gospelrum, which is none other than the traditional one, namely: Matthew, Mark, Luke and John (1, 2, 3; 2,46,95), to which he systematically adheres. But, apart from the generic ordo narrandi (1, 2, 4; 2, 21, 53; 2,30,70; 2, 43, 91; 3,2,8; 3, 5, 17), or ordo narrationis (2, 78, 153; 3,13,48; 3, 25, 80), Augustine points out others, more specific.

This is the ordo verborum (hyperbaton), or placement of the words within the period (2, 12, 27; 2, 12, 28; 2,12,29; 2, 14, 31; 2, 25, 57; 2, 62, 121; 2, 80, 157; 3,2,7); of the ordo temporum, which refers to the data that in transitus link some events with others (2, 21, 52; 2, 22, 53; 2,23,54; 2, 68, 131; 2, 78, 153); of the ordo rei gestae (rerum gestarum) or historical concatenation of events (2, 22, 53; 2,30,70; 2, 34, 81; 2, 36, 83; 2,39,86; 2,40,87; 2, 41, 88; 2, 42, 90; 2, 43, 91; 2, 44, 92; 2, 49, 103; of the ordo recollectionis, or order with which previously known events return to memory (2, 23, 54; 2,30,70; 2, 31, 78; 2,32,79; 2, 34, 81; 2, 41, 88; 2,42,90; 2, 53, 108); of the ordo sententiarum (2, 77, 147); of the ordo consequens (2, 42, 89). And referring to specific contents, he speaks of the ordo generatium (2,3,5) or the ordo vocationis (2,17,39). The ordo narrationis is evident in each evangelist; It is the personal concatenation that he makes of the events he narrates. This ordo narrationis in many cases reflects the ordo remembrationis more than the ordo rerum. In this regard, Augustine establishes a general principle: the ordo narrationis does not imply the ordo rerum (2, 21, 51). The ordo rerum gestarum is something objective; but the ordo reminder

nis is something subjective, the result of two subjectivities: that of the writer who remembers and that of God who directs those memories; hence the divergence in the order among the evangelists. Divergence that sometimes extends, and for the same reasons, to the ordo verborum, even within the same ordo rerum. Furthermore, a true ordo rerum does not presuppose a perfect ordo sententiarum (2,77,147). Given this state of affairs, Augustine positions himself at the level of principles and at the level of practice, since the different ordo can lead some to believe that there is contradiction between the evangelists (3,25,70). At the level of principles, he affirms that those who believe that, simply because one event is narrated after another, it happened after it, are in error (2,47,100). In relation to what interests him and constitutes the objective of the work, he also affirms, and repeatedly, that the different ordo in no way damages the veracity of the evangelists. The different order does nothing to affect the truth, just as the fact that one is silent about what another says does nothing to it (3,8,34; 3,18,55). For now, the different ordo (verborum or rerum) does not imply any contradiction (2,12,27; 2,77,147); Changing the ordo verborum in no way is equivalent to lying (2,12,28), nor does it in any way affect the admission of an evangelical sentence (2,13,41). Nor does following the ordo remembrationis contradict the ordo rerum (2,53,108; 2,72,140). Nor should the different ordo narrationis be a cause for concern, as long as the truth of what is narrated is maintained (2,16,33; 2,66,122) and there is no internal contradiction or with another evangelist (2,21,51 -52). In the event that such a contradiction appears to exist, it is necessary to consider the problem and seek a solution, in the certainty that it exists (2,21,52). From here it shows that it is uninteresting, and even superfluous, to look for, for example, the order in the Lord's speeches, since the order in which it appears has nothing to affect the truth of a story (ipsius ordinis nihil interest ad rem) (2,39,86). At the level of practice, in specific cases, without explicitly stating it, he thinks that the divergence is more apparent than real in the sense that the ordo is only broken by digressions (2,76,146; 3,6,21.24), although it cannot always be clearly determined whether it is a digression or not (2,75,145).

However, he cannot deny serious divergences in the order; In those cases he shows that they in no way imply contradiction in the facts themselves, resorting to three principles. One, that the way of proceeding of the evangelists must be taken into account, who sometimes present their stories as if they were an uninterrupted succession of events, without alluding to the fact that others have been omitted (2,25,58); another, that the Lord said or did the same thing several times and that, therefore, the respective accounts can respond to the ordo rerum even if they appear in different contexts (2,30,76; 2,32,79; 2,66,122; cf. complementary note 24: Repeated data); Finally, that the evangelists may be following a different ordo, one the ordo rerum and another the ordo remembranceis. When he chooses this last path, his consideratio strives to determine in each case which author follows the ordo rerum and which the ordo remembranceis, starting from the presupposition of the truth of the

gospels and that there is an objective ordo rerum that the four evangelists narrate. The main point of support to establish who follows one ordo and who another is found in the transitus from one narratio to another. The ordo rerum (gestarum) is established by Augustine based on the ordo temporum (2,22,53), with a procedure that sometimes appears excessively slave to the letter (2,23,54; 2,39,86). Just as on certain occasions the transitus indicates that the different evangelists follow a different ordo, in other cases it shows that the ordo narrationis and the ordo rerum coincide (2,28,64; 2,41,88; 2,42,89; 2,48,102). The coincidences between several evangelists are another criterion to determine the ordo (2,41,88). The same transitus favors the determination of the ordo in that it allows us to notice that there are spaces left to insert what one evangelist left out and another did not (2,28,64). However, there will be no shortage of cases in which it is impossible to determine whether it is one ordo or another (2,31,78), since we come across evangelical stories that appear devoid of any connection with what came before or what came after (2,41,88). But the difficulties do not end with determining that in a given case an evangelist follows the ordo remembranceis. There is still one more step, that is, to find out if the author recovers something that had been left behind (recolere-recapitulatio) or if he rather anticipates something that took place later (praeoecupatio) (2,30,70; cf. supplementary note 23: -Praeoccupatio-Recapitulatio»). Furthermore, the ordo allows us to see if a similar story present in several evangelists refers to a single fact or to several (2,71,139), although sometimes doubt persists (2,74,141). It is not difficult to understand that the statement is a derivation of the prejudice that there can be no falsehood in the gospels. Where there is no harmonization for the ordo, it solves the problem by multiplying the facts using the same ordo. Beyond the ordo narrationis, a combination of ordo rerum and ordo remembranceis, that each sacred author wanted to maintain, the ordo rerum was unique, and four times in the work Augustine proposed to establish that ordo rerum, or as he calls, a narratio: regarding the stories of infancy (2,5,16), the Bethany scene (2,78,153), the passion (3,2,8; 3,3,9) and of the appearances of the risen Lord (3,25,71).

As breaches of the ordo rerum, Augustine mentions both the praeoecupatio and the recapitulatio (cf. supplementary note 23: «Praeoecupatio-Recapitulatio •>). The evangelists are not always as explicit as could be desired, and sometimes they leave gaps. For example, it does not appear in the accounts of the apostles in what order the apostles were called (2,17,39) [7] Mark. The evangelist Mark occupies second place in the ordo gospelrum known to Augustine (1,2,3; 2,46,95). He was not an apostle and, consequently, he was not a direct witness of the acts and sayings of the Lord that he narrates. It was divine Providence, through the Spirit, that gave him authority to announce and write his gospel; His source of information is the apostles themselves (1,1,2; Sermo 239,1,1). He wrote in Greek (1,2,4). He did not want to narrate the lineage of Jesus; No

However, it preferably deals with what Christ did as a man. Regarding traditional symbology, Augustine considers that it is most accurately represented by the human figure, although he knows of others who prefer the figure of the eagle for him (1, 6, 9; 4, 10, 11; cf. also In lo. ev. 36, 5). Like Matthew and Luke, and in contrast to John, who usually flies in the heights, Mark, in what is related to Jesus, walks on the earth (4,10,15; In lo. ev. 36, 5). Like them, he is concerned above all with the humanity of Jesus Christ (4, 10, 11). In fact, he walks with both, because although he agrees with Matthew in many things, in some others he is more in line with Luke, thus corresponding to the human figure that represents him, which, referred to Christ, includes both the royal function, indicated by Matthew, and the priestly one, indicated by Luke (4, 10, 11). Augustine here seems to ignore the entire patristic tradition linking Mark to the apostle Peter. Some, like Papias (EUSEBIUS OF CAESÁREA, Hist. Eccles. 3,39,15), Irenaeus (Adversus Haereseslll 1,1) or Clement of Alexandria (EUSEBIUS, Hist. Eccles. 6,14,5-7), specifically make him an interpreter of Peter; others consider him more generically their follower (EPIPHANIO, Panarion 51, 6, 10; THEODORUS OF MOPSUESTIA, Commentary on the Gospel of the Apostle John 7, and JOHN CHRYSOSTOMO, Homilies on the Gospel of Matthew 1,2). On the contrary, in a judgment that is more of a literary than historical nature, he places him in a special relationship with Matthew, of whom he considers him pedisequus et breviator (1,2,4; 1,3,6) and comes (4, 10, 11), giving an explanation. As Matthew makes it his personal objective to expose the royal function of Christ, and kings usually have an entourage, so he takes Mark to his side (1, 3, 6; 4,10,11). The relationships, at a literary level, with the other apostles are explained clearly and accurately in a text: -What is exclusively his is very little. Only with Juan he has nothing in common. In few things he agrees only with Luke, and, on the other hand, with Matthew he agrees in many things, either with him alone, or also with the others; and in many of them with almost the same words" (1,2,4). At a literary level, Augustine highlights, as far as narratio is concerned, one quality: brevitas.

Throughout the pages, he highlights it again and again (2, 62, 122; 2, 64, 124; 3, 4, 11; 3, 8, 33; 3, 13, 47; 3, 25, 71. 75; 4, 3, 4), to the point of having to conclude by saying of him that he is maxime breviiatis sectator (3, 13, 47); the breviterperstringere is their usual way of proceeding (sicut adsolet - more suo: 3, 25, 75). This procedure is not a pure spontaneous attitude, but a conscious reality: more suo breviter commemorare voluisse (3, 25, 75; cf. supplementary note 22: "Narratio brevis et aperta"). Compared to the others, from the point of view of narratio brevis, Marcos occupies the top. A maximally explicit text: "Let us think how briefly Mark said this in comparison to Matthew, how briefly Matthew compared to Luke, how briefly Luke compared to John, and, finally, how briefly John compared to what happened" (3, 13, 47). The text refers to the specific case of the Lord's passion, but indicates the global truth regarding the evangelists. In fact, he repeats the same assessment in another context:

Just as Luke is more verbose than Matthew, Matthew is more verbose than Mark (2, 40, 87). To begin with, it is the breviator of Matthew (1, 2, 4; 2,30,70: 2, 76, 146), with whom, on the other hand, it is frequently on a par in said brevitas (2, 17, 37; 3,6,24; 3,7,27; 3, 16, 53). To the point that Augustine argues from the desire for brevity to affirm something, since the opposite would mean admitting that he wrote something superfluous (3, 2, 7). In some cases, however, he abandons his concern for narratio brevis, and gives in to the demands of clarity (distinctius-expréssius-planius) (3,2,7; 3,4,11); However, sometimes he prefers the dark expression. For example, regarding the authors of the crucifixion of the Lord, what John says clearly, Mark prefers to say it in a mysterious way (occulte) (3,13,42). Always at a literary level, Augustine warns that he combines indirect speech (ex verbis suis) with direct speech (verba ipsa domini) (3, 4, 13), or that, like Matthew, he resorts to syllepsis, although, as is his norm, he does not use the term -technical- (3, 16, 53). [8] Adoption. The harmonization of genealogies was important to Augustine. It was not just another objection that came from the ranks of the opposition. Giving it a solution undoubtedly meant some personal revenge. Augustine fell into Manichaeism not so much because he had been disappointed by the poor style of the Scriptures but because in the examination of Catholic Scripture (Confessiones 3,5,9) he did not find in them the necessary internal coherence (cf. P. No doubt under pressure from Manichean propaganda he read the genealogies (Sermo 51, 5, 6), and realizing the truth of Manichean criticism was passed on to the sect. The objection was at the very door of entry to the "Christian Scriptures" and it was easy to come across it: Matthew and Luke contradicted each other. The difficulty was perceived by many others before Augustine. Origen indicates that it had greatly disturbed some (Homilies on Luke 28). The solution took only one path. Julius Africanus solves the difficulty by resorting to the law of levirate (Gen 38,8; Dt 25,5-6; Mt 22, 24; Le 20, 28).

According to her, Joseph would be the natural son of Jacob (Mt) and the legal son of Heli (Le), since, when he died without children, Jacob would have married the widow and given her offspring. The explanation he provides is preserved for us by Eusebius of Caesarea, who transcribes his Letter to Aristeas (Eccl. History 1,7,2-16). This solution is appropriated by Eusebius himself (Quaestiones ad Stephanum 3), Hilary of Poitiers (In Matthaeum 1,1: SC 254, 92), Apollinaris of Laodicea 0. This solution, however, is decisively rejected by Ambrosiaster, indicating that nec probabile est et ad nullam rem proficit (Liber quaestionum Veteris et Novi Testamenti. Appendix quaestionum Novi Testamenti 56, 1).
