den of David, one can speak of the Savior being the son of both one and the other (ipsa enim ratione qua Ioseph films dicitur Salvator, ipsa est et Helifilius et ceterorum omnium, qui de eadem tribu sunt) (ib., in H. MERKEL, Diepluralitát,

Origen, who makes a much more detailed analysis than Augustine of the variants between the genealogies offered by Matthew and Luke, is content to justify them from the different intention that dominated the story of each evangelist (Homilies on Luke 28). In addition to the one at hand, Augustine addresses it in numerous other texts, the following in chronological order: De diversis quaestionibus LXXXni,6l,2: PL40,49; ContraFaustum 3.3: CSEL 25/1, 264; Quaestiones gospelrum 2.5: PL 35,1334-1335; Sermo 51,17,27;19,29: PL 38,348; Quaestiones in Heptateuchum 5.46: CSEL 28/2.404; Retractationes 2,42,2: CSEL 36/2,150-151. The solutions offered are the following: In De div. quaest., without entering directly into the problem, explains the diversity in terms of the double function, royal and priestly, of Christ. In Contra Faustum the quaestio quomodo potuerit duos habere paires Joseph is already explicitly stated. That is, he says, the problem, because once it is recognized that he has had two parents, the other divergences in the family tree are explained. He finds the solution by resorting to adoption, whose existence he demonstrates in the Jewish people: one evangelist expressed adoptive paternity and another natural paternity. He also alludes to other solutions, but without explaining them. In the Quaestiones gospelrum he offers three alternative solutions: adoption, the law of levirate, origo maiorum; That is, one evangelist gives the name of the father and another the name of other ancestors through the maternal branch. Of the three, that of the levirate seems inconsistent to him (he confirms), due to the fact that the son bore the name of the deceased. In sermo 51 he once again presents the three possibilities mentioned in the previous text: the origo maiorum, the law of adoption and the law of levirate, which he accepts here without reservation. In Quaestiones in Heptateuchum he dispenses with the origo maiorum and, while maintaining the preferred solution of adoption, fully accepts that of the levirate. Finally, in Retractationes he interprets adoption as adoption in favor of a dead person, that is, he merges the legal path of adoption and levirate into one; levirate is nothing but a form of adoption. [9] Objective of the work. As can be seen from the title of the work, it is clear that the thesis defended by Augustine in it is that of the harmony of the four evangelists among themselves and with each other.

He refers to his intended objective on more than one occasion, especially in the face of the temptation to deviate from it by pursuing other matters, such as, for example, why the Holy Spirit acts in some in one way and in others in another (2,21,52), the exposition of the gospels (2,27,151), the theology of the mystical Body (3,4,14), or Trinitarian doctrine (4,10,19). The resources used are included in the general introduction, and some of them are developed more fully in these complementary notes. The language used has a double aspect, which we can designate as objective line and subjective line. The first emphasizes the objective agreement of the narrative contents of

one and the other author. In the second, it is the authors who confirm each other. To affirm his position on the problem, Augustine resorts to the terminology of his opponents, of course in a negative formulation: in his pages we find contrarium, adversan, repugnare, discrepare, dissentire, dissonare, and discordare, etc., obviously preceded by non. But this is only one part, since just as frequently he resorts to the positive formulation that changes dis- for con-: dissentire is opposed to consent; to dissonare, the consonare; when discordare the concordare, next to concinno. Nothing better than the preposition cum, the preposition of the company, to indicate the together and harmonious walk of the four evangelists, in addition to the apostle Paul. The terms are best understood if placed in the field of literary criticism. Although what worries Augustine and what he intends is nothing more than to show the harmony between the evangelists, he does so not from categorical statements, but from literary analysis. For a narratio - and the gospel is a narratio - to be credible, it must achieve the congruence of its elements. This is what the terms indicated above clearly express, to which the verb congruere can be added; Although its presence in Augustinian work is not as frequent as that of the others, it is significant because of the place where it is placed. The objective indicated at the beginning of the second book, in which the examination of the gospels begins, is to see - how sibi adque Inter se congruant what the four evangelites wrote about Christ -, to avoid obstacles infide cbristiana, facing the accusation of inconvenientia and repugnantia (2,1). This Christian fides does not refer to theological virtue, but to the credibility that Christians assign to the gospels. The same must be said of the term convenire/convenientia, which appears in another key place: at the end of the first book, where it also indicates the purpose that animates it, which is none other than to show how the apostles show themselves in harmony (concordia) to the convenientia scribando (1,35,54). The same thing appears in another important moment, at the beginning of the third book: videtur mihi expeditius nos demonstrare posse omnium evangelistarum convenientiam, si ab hoc iam loco omnium omnia contexamus et in unam narrationem faciemque digeramus (3,1) (cf. H. LAUSBERG, Manual, n.289).

The narratio evangelica deserves credibility based on the harmony and "congruence" of its elements. The other line, which we call subjective, is placed more in a judicial context, where witnesses have a special weight in order to determine the truth. Thus one or more evangelists testantur, adtestantur, contestantur or cotestantur to another or others. [10] The gospels as ^narratio». Both the noun narratio and the verb narrare appear continuously in the De consensu. The gospels are for him a narratio, obviously literary. But the term narratio does not always have the same extension. Sometimes it refers to what in exegetical language is called pericope (2,28,65: in hac ergo narratione), other times to each gospel (passim); In other cases Augustine thinks about the possibility of a narratio elaborated with the material provided by the narrations of the other evangelists (2,5,17; 2,6,18).
Supplementary Notes

The activity of the evangelist is designated by Augustine as a narrare. To refer to the elaboration specifically, he uses the expression contexere narrationem (passim). Narrationes that vary from one to another both by the detractions, in particular the praeteritiones (passim; cf. H. LAUSBERG, Manual, n. 882-886), and by the adiectiones they experience, consisting of an infinite number of interpositiones (in the substantive or verbal form there are about 40 uses; cf. H. LAUSBERG, Manual, n. 860), inferences (inferre: 2, 6, 18. 19; 3, 4, 11), subnexions (2, 38, 85; 2, 54, 110; 3,1,2; 3,2,5; cf. H. LAUSBERG, Manual, n. 861), aetiologiae (3, 1, 2; Manual, n. 867); adnexions (2,39,86; 2,55,111) and digressions (2, 75, 144. 145; 2, 48, 102; 3,8,34; cf. H. LAUSBERG, Manual, n. 340-342), and above all by the ordo (cf. complementary note 6: "Ordo"). Augustine is especially attentive to the transitus (cf. H. LAUSBERG, Manual, n. 849) through which the different elements that make up the narratio are articulated (2, 28, 64; 2, 40, 87; 2, 41, 88; 2, 42, 89; 2, 43, 91, 2, 48, 102). and they serve him in a special way to establish whether in a given case the evangelist follows the ordo rerum or the ordo remembranceis. As a narrator, each evangelist has his own modus narrandi (2, 19, 47; 2, 72, 121), which consists of nothing more than the diverse literary way of presenting the material without affecting the truth of what is narrated. The statement seems to imply the literary differentiation of each author, and could give the importance of full autonomy in this regard, but it is not entirely accurate. Indeed, the diversity in the modus narrandi has its maximum expression in the ordo narrandi, which does not depend absolutely and fully on the will of the evangelist, but on his memory and, ultimately, on God who regulates it (cf. complementary notes 6: "Ordo" and 15: Memory). In this sense the evangelical narratio has its rules (cf. complementary note 11: "Regulae"), which do not always coincide with those of the profane narratio; rules that have a transcendent inspiration, from the Spirit, and it would be the fruit of arrogance to try to impose others (leges) on the veritatis narrators (3, 13, 48). However, the evangelists have their personality as narrators.

In his consideratio Augustine highlights that Mark seeks above all the virtus of the narratio brevis, in which Matthew frequently accompanies him, while Luke chooses to give preference to the narratio aperta (cf. supplementary note 22: "Narratio brevis et aperta"), or habitually resorts to the praeoccupatio (cf. supplementary note 23: "Praeoccupatio-Recapitulatio"), while John stands out for his sublime language. Beyond what may be personal characteristics of each evangelical narrator, all evangelical narrations are true (2, 6, 18; 2, 12, 29), and all evangelists are qualified as veridici narratores (2, 46, 97), narratores veritatis (3, 13, 48; cf. complementary note 16: Truth), despite their narrations vary among themselves (2, 12, 28). [11] “Regulae”. If we speak of regulae it is only out of fidelity to Augustinian terminology (2, 20, 50; 2, 46, 95. 96; 2, 66, 127; 2, 79, 155; 3, 20, 57). We could talk about the criteria that Augustine takes into account and that, applied, provide the solution to the criticisms of contradiction that come from outside the Christian faith. In this note we limit ourselves

to the cases in which the criterion is explicitly mentioned, not to its application, which is considered in other complementary notes. Thus, to avoid difficulties, the reader must take into account the following principles: 1. Each evangelist weaves his story as if it were a continuous sequence that does not omit anything; Although he remains silent about what he is not interested in saying, he links things together in such a way that it gives the impression of a story of consecutive events (2, 5, 16; 2, 25, 58; 3, 25, 73; 3, 13, 44). The attentive reader will notice, after analyzing the order, the place where what one author is silent about, but another author mentions, has a place. Cf. complementary note 6: «Ordo». 2. The fact that an author conceals what another says in no way violates the truth (2, 6, 18; 2, 19, 47; 2,20,50; 2,46,96; 3,8,34; 3, 18, 55; 3,20,57; 4, 10, 11). Cf. complementary note 16: Truth. 3. There is no contradiction in the fact that someone says in one way what another has said in a different way, as long as it is to clarify the truth of the resy sententiae (2,19 A7) or, in any case, it does not depart from the same statement (2, 27, 63; 2, 28, 65; 3, 4, 13). The varietas does not imply adversitas ( 3, 4, 13 ). Cf. complementary note 14: “Sententia”. 4. What is important and what must always be sought is the will of the author; Consequently, there is no lie even when someone puts something that was not said by the person to whom he refers, as long as he exposes his will (2, 12, 29; 2, 46, 97; 3, 4, 14). That is why it is superfluous to look for the ipsissima verba, once the sententia is known (3,2,8). Cf. complementary note 20: “Voluntas”. 5. Nothing affects the truth if one author uses vulgar language and another uses his own language, as long as he maintains the same statement (2, 28, 65), or one author uses his own language and another uses figurative language (2, 30, 77). Words, in their materiality, lose interest as long as they are of the same value in order to the same truth of the statement (2, 24, 55). Cf. complementary note 28: "Locutio figurata". 6. Noting the possible polysemy of terms can be the beginning of solving some difficulties (2, 30, 72; 2, 30, 74). Cf. complementary note 28: "Locutio figurata". 7.

He repeatedly affirms that the order in which each evangelist wanted or was able to present his stories does not affect the truth (2, 21, 52; 2, 62, 121; 2,39,86; 3, 8, 34). Cf. complementary note 6: «Ordo». 8. It does not follow from the fact that one thing is narrated after another that it happened afterwards (2, 21, 51). Cf. complementary note 6: «Ordo». 9. The diverse narrandi modus does not affect the truth (2, 62, 121). Cf. complementary note 16: Truth. 10. The Lord's acts and sayings were not unique, but he was able to repeat both of them. Consequently, when they are difficult to harmonize with each other, it is worth thinking that they are not the same, but rather identical ones (2, 29, 69; 2,30,76; 2, 32, 79; 2,51,106; 2, 61, 120; 2, 79, 155). In this regard, the case of the multiplication of the loaves is instructive: if Matthew, instead of the two, had only narrated the one that Mark is silent about, one would have thought that it was contradicted.

The sacred author may have used rhetorical figures among which the synecdoche (2,46,97; 2,66,127; 2,79,155; 3,24,66), syllepsis or antonomasia, wave recapitulatio and prolepsis stand out. Cf. complementary notes 27: Synecdoche and 23: -Praeoccupatio-Recapitulatio». In one way or another, all these principles are included in this programmatic text: We should not think that someone is lying if, after hearing or seeing something, when they remember it they do not refer to it in the same way or with the same words; if the order of these changes; if you use some words for others of identical meaning; if something is left out that either does not come to mind to the person trying to remember it or can be deduced from what was said; if, based on other interests, you simply touch something without the intention of developing it in its entirety; if, for greater clarity, he adds other words, or if, despite trying, a textual reproduction is not achieved (2,12,28). The first thing one notices after considering these principles is that, in practice, they all fall into the realm of literary criticism or grammaticus. Augustine calls them regulae locutionum applicable to similar cases, given that through different expressions the same statement and the same truth of things are maintained (2,46,95). He only resorts to the possibilities or freedoms that every author has when composing a text: freedoms regarding the content of the narratio, that is, freedom to introduce one fact or another; freedom with respect to the order, that is, to place it in one place or another; freedom regarding the verba, to play with their number, with their order, with their meaning, with their use; freedom to resort to rhetorical figures. Whoever knows how to perceive all this will not find any difficulty.' As we said, we are not dealing here primarily with Augustinian praxis, but with the principles (regulae) that he formulates as such. Augustine formulates them referring to a specific case so that they have general validity and apply to other parallel cases (2,5,16; 2,6,18; 2,46,96.97; 2,61,120; 2,66,127). For this purpose, he himself recommends them, orders them to be diligently archived in memory and invites them to be remembered when the time comes (2, 12, 29; 2, 29, 69; 2,46,95.96.97).

He frequently refers to previous mentions (2,19,47; 2,20,50; 2,51,106; 2,61,120; 2,79,155) and even feels a certain discomfort every time he has to do so (2,30,76; 2,61,120; 3,13,49). He does not consider these rules as personal discoveries or as the result of special preparation, but as something within everyone's reach, which everyone can see spontaneously (2,19,47); that it is sufficiently visible (2,27,63); or that appears with sufficient clarity (2,46,97); with reference to a rule he will affirm that it is notissima (3,20,57). There is nothing strange about his statement that whoever does not notice it is either daring or unerudite (temeré e inerudite) (2,30,76). These last words are significant. Eruditio was the content of the scientific culture of the time (Cf. H. I. MARROU, Saint Augustin et la fin déla culture antique [Paris 1938.], p.l46.559ss). The conclusion is that to maintain that there are contradictions in the gospels is to place

left the culture. Which indicates the area in which Augustine has placed himself in solving the problems. He has simply acted as a grammarian who comments on a text from the grammarians' principles. [12] «Tempus». The tempus circumstance becomes for Augustine, in some cases, a source of difficulties, and in others, a channel for solution, always with reference to the objective of the work, that is, to show that there is no contradiction between the evangelists. Indeed, sometimes the difficulty in harmonizing evangelical stories comes from chronological data; One case is that referred to Herod (Mt 2, 19 and L c 3, l). The solution is found by Augustine showing that this difficulty is only apparent, since it arises from not taking into account that these are two characters with the same name, successive in time, Herod the king and Herod the tetrarch (2,7,20). Augustine often repeats that the different ordo does not in itself affect the truth of the story (cf. complementary note 6: -Ordo*). However, the consideration of the just ordo temporis is constant in him, and sometimes he wastes ingenuity in the effort to determine it, because it is for him an effective means in solving the objections of his enemies. We have examples of this in his examination of the Gethsemane scene (3,5,17), Peter's denials (3,6,21-23) and the trial of Jesus (3,7,27). On some occasions he even resorts to popular language to explain the chronological data and show that there is a coincidence, despite the apparent discrepancy (3,24,65). Undoubtedly forcing the text, the absence of explicit chronological data allows him to place a fact where it seems best and thus manages to combine the data (3,25,80). The recourse to the tempus circumstance allows him to show that the disagreement between different evangelical accounts is only apparent and, therefore, non-existent. In this way it solves numerous difficulties; for example, those presented by Le 2,41 and Mt 2,22 (2,10,13), or Le 5,10b on the one hand and Mt 4,19, Me l,17 and jn 1,35-44 on the other (2,17,37). Noting that Luke 9:9 and Mt 14:2 refer to two different moments, the divergence is canceled (2,43,91). The same can be said of Mt 22,35b and Mark 12,34b (he entered with bad intentions and changed, corrected by the Lord) (2,73,141).

The contradiction between Mt 26,46 and Mt 26,45b is annulled by spacing the moments chronologically (3,4,11), the same as that existing between Mt 27,55, Mark 15,40 and Le 23,49 on one part and Jn 19,25 on the other (3,21,58), or that existing between Le 24,4 and Jn 20,12 (3,24,69), or between Le 24,12 and Jn 20,5-6 (3,25,70), between Le 24,33 and Jn 20,24 (3,25,75); or between Jn 19,17a on the one hand and Mt 27,32, Mark 15,20b-21 and Le 23-26 on the other (3,10,17). Augustine starts from a fact that he gives the character of a principle applicable to different cases, namely: that each evangelist composes his story as if it were a continuous sequence, which did not omit anything; who, keeping silent about what he does not want to say, adds to the above what he does want, giving the impression of a continuous story (2,5,16). Cf. VOGELS, St. Augustin Schrifts, 117-130. [13] «Quaestio». When in book I, after the long digression that is 7,11-33,51, he returns to the purpose that moved him to compose the work (propositam intentionem), he presents it as an attempt to answer (solvere) to the different questions that, regarding the concordance

The very conclusion of the book first once again indicates the objective, which is none other than to provide a solution to these questions (quaestionibus dissolutis), so that full concord appears (1, 35, 54). The objective that has been set in the writing is nothing other than to elucidate the profound question of harmony between the gospels (huic tam magnae quaestioni quam de consensu evangelistarum enodandam suscepimus (2,42,90). Although the title does not suggest it, the work is globally placed within the genre of quaesttones et solutions, present in patristic biblical literature (cf. Quaestiones gospelrum, De diversis quaestionibus ad Simplicianum, Quaestiones in Heptateuchum). from the point of view of harmony and concord among the sacred authors. Dealing with the quaestiones is not due to scholarly interest, but to pastoral interest; in fact, they disturb the faith of those who are already believers and are an impediment to the access to it of those who are still unbelievers; in addition, there are no shortage of Christians who want to know what should be answered to them (1,7,10). quaestio as a fact, as a possibility, as a custom. That is to say, frequently the transitus from one point to another is simply formulated as a quaestio: quaeritur (2, 12, 27; 2, 15, 32); 2, 30, 71).

Formulated negatively, it is a quaestio repugnantiae, with respect to which Augustine limits himself to stating, in general and in particular, that it does not exist (2,34,81; 2,41,88; 2,49,103; 2,58,116; 2,70,134; 2,72,140; 4,5,6), just as with respect to the quaestio dissensionis (3,23,60). Augustine reads the text from the concern of the possible quaestio. In many cases it does not find any: nulla quaestio est (2, 77, 152; 2, 79, 156; 2, 80, 158; 3, 8, 35; 3, 25, 85; 4, 1, 2), or it does not remain (3, 24, 64). Sometimes the quaestio is superfluous (2, 39, 86), but other times it is non contemnenda (3, 24, 65). In any case, the questions are numerous. The magna quaestio is the result of an endless number of concrete quaestiones, whose types are multiple: referring to the quando (2, 5, 16), to the quomodo (2,11,24; 2,15,32; 2,17,41; 2,30,71) or quemadmodum (2, 15, 32), to the "ipsissima" verba of an author ( 2, 12, 27. 29; 2, 14, 31); we come across the quaestio de loco (2, 25, 58), de tempore (3, 24, 65; 3, 25, 79), de ordine (2, 58, 116; 2, 39, 86), all of them referring to various evangelical passages. systematic treatment, but the result

state of reading the text itself. There is a diversity of categories among the questions; Some tend to especially encourage the shamelessness of contentious people and disturb the ignorance of the weak (3, 13, 50). The texts indicated here refer to those where Augustine explicitly mentions the word quaestio. But the appearance of the term is not required to perceive its presence. The terminology of the quaestio solution is not very varied; It is collected in the three verbs enodare, solvere, dissolvere. Regarding the solution itself, Augustine starts from the prejudice of the truth of the gospels (cf. complementary note 16: Truth). Which means that every quaestio or difficulty must have a solution, that is, there must be ways to harmonize all evangelists. And if a solution does not convince, it is necessary to look for another, knowing that it exists. The quaestio, in turn, can admit several solutions (2, 9, 22; 3,13,43). The criterion in any of them must always be that it does not give rise to another quaestio repugnantiae (2, 77, 152). In fact, a quaestio not rarely manifests itself as being a series of quaestiones, so that when one has been resolved, it remains unresolved or a new one appears (2, 25, 58). This solution sometimes offers difficulty, other times it does not (2, 10, 23). The solution given to one quaestio becomes a criterion for the solution of others (2, 65, 125). For these solution criteria, cf. complementary note 11: ~Regulae». The quaestio seems to refer to objective difficulty. When Agustín wants to present it in the subjective aspect, referring to third parties, he always uses the verb moveré. It is nothing more than indicating in different ways that a quaestio exists. It uses different formulas: that of the affirmation, both positive and negative (which means I will move nonnullos, or other similar ones: 2,7,20; 2, 46, 97; 2,50,105; 2, 70, 135); that of possibility ( comopotest moveré 2, 17, 37; 2,19,45; 2, 26, 48; 2,35,82; 2,46,96; 2, 66, 128; 3, 24, 63 ); the conditional (as nisi forte quispiam moveatur 2, 8. 21; 2, 21, 52; 3,2,5; 3,7,293,25,75).

On numerous occasions, however, Augustine goes ahead to warn that no difficulty should be felt, even if it might seem that there is reason for it (2, 12, 25; 2,46,96; 2, 51, 106; 2,66,127; 2, 70, 137; 2, 73, 141; 3,2,7; 3,5,17; 3, 17, 54). But there is no shortage of cases in which he claims that perceiving the difficulty is justified ( 3, 22, 59 ). Sometimes it specifies the subjects in whom this move occurs, indicating from there the solution (2, 53, 108), or even the cause from which the perception of the difficulty originates; It lies solely in the subject's lack of understanding (2, 78, 153). Therefore, the attitude towards these subjects who feel it should not be, Augustine warns, that of contempt, but rather that of an effort to instruct them (2, 56, 113). [14] “Sententia”. When Cicero indicates (De optimal genere oratorum 2,4) that eloquence consists of verbay sententiae, he establishes a distinction that runs through the entire De consensu. The one who speaks, and by extension the one who writes, communicates a thought (sententia) and to communicate it uses the medium of words (verba). The above is not the only meaning of sententia. Another, more specific, is the one that equates them to the Greek gnomes (QIUNT., Instit. Orat. 8,5,3). The author of the Rhetorica ad Herennium defines it as oratio

sumpta de vita, quae aut quid sit aut quid esse oporteat in vita breviter ostendit ( 4, 17, 24; cf. Rhetorica ad C. Herennium. Introduzione, testo criticalo, commento a cura di G. Calboli [Bologna 1969], note 102, p.325ff). Saint Isidore identifies it with a dictum impersonale (Etymologiae 2, 11, 1; cf. H. LAUSBERG, Manual, n. 872-879 and passim). It is characterized, therefore, by a tone of universality (Saint Isidore), as well as moralizing (Ad Herennium). In this meaning we must interpret many uses by Augustine. What modern exegetes call sayings and narrative material, Augustine designates with the terms sententia and res respectively. In keeping with the ample space that the evangelists dedicate to the teaching of Jesus, the term sententia appears frequently in the De consensu and becomes, together with the meaning indicated above, a key concept at the service of the objective of the work. By defining the teachings of Jesus as sententiae, Augustine may be indicating precisely that character of universality that surpasses the specific case, as well as its value in regulating life. In both cases, the sententiae, as well as the res, appear in Augustinian writing as opposed to the verba or other concepts that refer to expression. That is to say, the res and the sententiae refer to the permanent, to what we could call content, while the other to the exterior, to the mutable. Veritas is associated with res and sententia; These are the subject of it. The truth, he says, must not be sought or embraced in words, but in what they indicate (2, 12, 28). In contrast to veritas rerum et sententiarum there are literary aspects, and therefore mutable, such as locutio (2, 12, 28; 2, 46, 95); the modus narrandi (diverse narrandi mode, sed eadem vertíate rerum et sententiarum) (2, 19, 47); the modus dicendi (2, 19, 47; 2, 27, 62); the genus... modus (2, 80, 157). From here we understand Augustine's continued use of the concept as a resource to explain the variety of formulations among the evangelists without being able to accuse them of opposition or contradiction. Far from literal fidelity, evangelists may be saying the same thing, as long as they reproduce the meaning.

We have the example in this Augustinian text: -Whether he spoke of untying the strap of the shoe, or of wearing the shoe, everyone who, even in his own words, when mentioning the shoe, expressed that same meaning, namely, humility, maintained the same sententia" (2, 12, 29). Thus, variatio is possible in the words without changing the sententia (2, 12, 26). Verbal coincidence is not required for coincidence to occur in the sententia ( 3, 17, 54 ). One of Augustine's resources, and perhaps the most frequent, consists precisely in affirming the variatio in the words and identity in the sententiae. As an example, we see it applied to the words of the apostles during the storm (2, 24, 55); to those of the demons expelled from the pigs (2, 24, 56); to the question about fasting (2, 27, 61); to the question about David (2, 74, 143); to the announcement of Peter's denial (3, 2, 7), etc. In all cases, although a mutatio verbi is given, the same sententia is maintained (2,77,149). The variety of words is combined with the harmony of rerum and sententiarum. The verbal difference may be due to several reasons.
Additional notes

One of them: downplaying the importance of mutable words, showing that the use of one or the other lacks significance (2, 24, 55; 3,2,8); and at the same time, the other side of the coin, to show that what matters is the sententia, always identical in the different formulations, and that it is this that must be sought (3, 4, 14). Expressed another way, it is to indicate that what must be sought is the will of the speaker (2, 46, 97), the voluntas sententiae (2, 70, 135). Other times it comes from demands for clarity (2, 27, 61; 2, 38, 85; 2, 19, 47). In fact, a statement is better "insinuated" when there is a variety of expression without altering the truth (2, 27, 61). The evangelists not only relate, but even try to explain the sententia, one in a shorter way, another in a longer way, and from this usually come differences between them (2, 12, 27). As an example, the variants in the account of the baptism of the Lord come from the desire to give a more familiar explanation of the sententia of the Lord ( 2, 12, 31 ). (eleganter) and with broader views ( 2, 27, 67 ). Sometimes, only the sum of the different forms of expression that a sententia acquires allows us to understand its meaning ( 3, 4, 13 ). same explained. The same thing that is affirmed of the words, is affirmed of the expressions (locutions): different locutions can refer to the same sententia (2, 14, 31; 2, 56, 112; 2, 66, 128). In the same way, the use of a usual language or a proper language does not affect it (2, 28, 65); 23, 54), regarding which we must always consider the possibility that the Lord has pronounced it on more than one occasion (2, 19, 43; 2, 64, 124; cf. complementary note 24: Repeated data).

To solve possible difficulties, it is also worth taking into account that two sententiae may have been merged into one (2, 46, 96; 3,1,2) or abbreviated (3, 4, 11). When the harmonization of two sententiae is problematic, it is possible to think that they are two different sententiae (3,6,25; 3,20,57). [15] Memory. The concept of memory, expressed in a variety of terms (meminisse, reminisci, rememberi), is one of the keys to this Augustinian work. Obviously, this is the memory of the apostles - evangelists. Augustine resorts to it to substantiate, although only in part, the truth of the gospels themselves. And this in two ways: both in the objective veracity of the narrated content and in the non-contradiction of the evangelists among themselves. To his memory we must attribute the veracity of the story and, as a negative element, the divergence in order between the different gospels. At the basis of the gospel and, consequently, of the gospels is the memory of the evangelists. This memory has behind it the personal experience of those who heard and saw Jesus personally and, in the case of those who were not eyewitnesses, serious information, gathered from those who could give it with guarantee, such as Jesus himself, his relatives or other witnesses worthy of all credit (1, 1, 1).
Additional notes

Each evangelist depended on his memory (ut meminerat) and his specific intentions (ut cuique cordi erat) when writing his stories (2, 12, 27). Just as Augustine denies any possibility of lying in the evangelist, he admits the possibility of forgetting, but as long as it is understood that this forgetting does not give rise to any falsehood (2, 12, 29). With the same forcefulness he denies the falsehood arising from lies and the deception resulting from forgetting (2, 50, 105). The memory of the evangelists, for its part, does not act autonomously as happens in other men, leaving aside ordinary providence. In it, in that of the evangelists, God intervenes in a particular way. In no case does the content or timing of his memories fall within man's power. But what in others is considered fortuitous, the evangelists attributed to the hidden power of God, who acts in it in a specific way with a view to the order of the narrative (3, 13, 48). Whether something came to mind of the evangelist did not depend on his will, but was a gift from God (2, 21, 51). The gift translates into governing and ruling the minds (resp. the hearts) of the sacred authors in the act of remembering what they were going to write, individually, not uniformly for all (2, 21, 52; 3, 13, 48). In other cases he presents this action as a suggestio divina to remember and write something previously known (2, 19, 44; 2, 21, 51). The ordo is another of the key concepts on which Augustinian work is based (cf. complementary note 6: "Ordo"). Now, in the configuration of that order, memory has a role of primary importance. It largely depends on her. As it says in a text already mentioned, man is not the owner of his memory; she acts outside of her own freedom and will. In that sense the evangelist is her servant. It is frequent that the data is provided at the wrong time, either late, and then the evangelist has to -recover- what was forgotten, or in advance, and then "anticipates" (praeoccupat) what happened subsequently (2, 19, 44; 2, 21, 51; cf. complementary note 23: "Praeoccupatio-Recapitulatio"). It is not always certain whether in a specific case of divergence between two evangelists it is one thing or the other (2, 23, 54; 2, 30, 70).

This dislocation, the result of the functioning of memory, is not an exceptional case, but common in the different evangelists: Matthew (2, 20, 48; 2, 21, 51; 2, 22, 53; 2, 26, 59; 2, 27, 60; 2, 32, 79; 2, 42, 89; 2, 53, 109; 3, 13, 44); Mark (2, 38, 85; 2, 68, 131); Luke (2, 20, 48; 2, 40, 87; 2,44,92; 2, 53, 108; 2, 75, 145; 2, 77, 152; 3, 25, 70); Mark/Luke (2, 28, 64). With all these limitations, the evangelist (Augustine considers it quite probable) submits to its dictates, in a docile attitude, due to his faith in the above, namely, that God governs it (2, 21, 51). The order depends on memory, which is ruled and governed by God; therefore the order derives from God. Memory, on the other hand, is limited in the sense that the subject can remember the central core of the fact or the content of a statement, but not the details or exact words, hence the mutatio del ordo verborum, and the use of alia pro aliis with identical meaningful content. Someone might think that in such a case one must speak of a lie. Augustine's providential and moralistic mind makes him translate

use what happened to the evangelists as a moral lesson. They also suffered these limits and consequences of their memory, but, given their excellent authority, they cannot be accused in any way of having lied or deceived. The consequence he draws is the following: As it is not lawful to judge or affirm that any of the evangelists lied, so it will appear that neither did he lie to whom what happened in his memory what is shown to have happened to them (2, 12, 28). [16] Truth. The truth of the gospels is in De Consensus its starting point and arrival point for Augustine. It is a starting point thinking about himself; It is an immovable and indisputable principle for him, although not undisputed in fact. It is the arrival point, thinking about the recipients of the work. That is to say, with his writing Augustine does not intend anything other than to demonstrate the affirmed truth of the evangelical books. If there is a distinction between starting point and arrival point, it is because there is a space occupied by those who deny that truth, relying on, for Augustine, alleged internal contradictions or with respect to the other evangelists. For Augustine, this truth has a final transcendent foundation, which is none other than the government by the Spirit of the minds of the evangelists (cf. complementary note 18: Inspiration). Hence I can designate them as narratores veritatis (3, 13, 47); Furthermore, extremely truthful narrators (3, 25, 71). Hence also why laws cannot be imposed on them from outside (3, 17, 47). The evangelist is truthful not only in what he narrates, but also in what he judges, by virtue of which he takes his license (3, 13, 42). The truth of the gospels also has other less transcendent foundations, but no less solid. The evangelical authors were direct or indirect witnesses of the events narrated and, furthermore, they were approved first by the apostles themselves who, according to Augustine, were still alive at the time of the composition of the writings and then by the Church (4, 8, 9). That is, the great authority achieved in the Church is a guarantee of truth (cf. complementary note 1: Authority). But first the truth of the Gospel has obtained the summit of authority for the word of God (2, 12, 28). It is not possible, therefore, to derogate from the faith of the evangelist (3,7,29).

Augustine's statements are not usually general in nature, but rather refer to specific cases. That each Gospel account conforms to the truth is a constant affirmation (2, 3, 5; 2,6,18; 2, 12, 29, etc.). All falsehood is excluded, whether it could come from a lie or from forgetfulness, a forgetfulness that on the other hand can occur, as long as it does not entail falsehood for the story (2, 12, 29). Not perceiving this truth is the result of a personal attitude more inclined to accuse than to reflect on the data (2, 7, 20); of an intellectual behavior that proceeds from prejudices, without evidence, through which opposite positions would be arrived at in the same way (2, 79, 155); In fact, even the contentious subject, not only the faithful Christian, will perceive that truth in his reflection, regardless of what he proclaims (2, 65, 126). Hesitating between following the evangelists or following those who accuse them is like hesitating between going after the (divine) truth or going after human suspicions (3, 13, 43). For Augustine, despite all contrary appearances, the truth of the evangelical stories will become clear if only we take into account certain

procedures that regulate the conduct of their authors (2,6,18) (cf. complementary note 11: «Regulae»). In his effort to make the truth the point of arrival of his work, he does not rely so much on arguments of a theological, philosophical or historical nature, as much as those of a literary nature. Leaving aside personal prejudices and irrational attitudes, seeing contradictions among evangelists is a sign of a deficient literary culture. In fact, Augustine's greatest effort is aimed at showing how resorting to different literary devices in no way means endangering the truth. In other words, where some see contradictions, what the attentive reader perceives are those artifices. A programmatic text like 2,12,28 clearly indicates this. From it we highlight the following elements: non eodem moda adque eisdem verbis... ordo verborum, alia pro aliis... quod ex aliis possint intelligi... non totum sed ex parte... verborum additio... variari narrationes... non eadem locutione (2,12,28). The terminology places us before the analysis of a grammarian of antiquity. And just as no one will speak of falsehood or lies based on a variatio in the words or in the narration, a different ordo, a figurative language (of ellipses, intentional or not), the insinuatio, or whether something is left to deduction, as long as the same res or sententia is maintained, so one cannot speak of falsehood or lies in the evangelists. If we analyze the texts in which Augustine refers to the truth of the gospels, we see that in a large part of them it appears associated with literary concepts. In addition to the previously collected, we bring here: 2,19,47 (diverso narrandi moda... alio moda dicere); 2,21,51 (quo loco... ex ordine... recolere... praeoccupare); 2,28,65 (dicere usitate, dicere proprie); 2,30,72 (diversis significanceibtis); 2,46,95 (diversis locutionibus); 2,55,111 (eodem ordine... diverse verborum ordine); 2,57,115 (diversitas verborum); 2,62,121 (ordo vel modus verborum..., narrandi modus); 2,66,128 (in eloquy varying... different way); 2,80,157 (genus...modus; diversitas verborum); 3,8,24 (quo ordine).

We have, therefore, multiple reference to the ordo verborum, to the ordo narrationis (cf. complementary note 6: "Ordo"), to lapraeoccupatio (cf. complementary note 23: "Praeoccupatio-Recapitulatio"), to habitual language and proper language, to polysemy, to variatio andcopia verborum, etc., concepts from which it can be understood that there is no contradiction where appearances take that direction. In De consensu Augustine continually relativizes the materiality of words; We must not think, he says, that the truth is protected with magic words (consecratis sonis), because God does not make them as expensive as he does the bulls. Furthermore, if it could be achieved without them, they would disappear (2,66,128). The truth that must be sought and embraced does not require the identity of the words, but of the reí and the sententiae (2,12,28). Both of them remain immutable in their truth in the different evangelists, with mutability being reserved fundamentally for the ordo, the verba and the locutions. In fact, the terms mentioned above, which indicate the variant element, normally appear opposed to res and sententiae as a fixed element (2,12,28; 2,16,33;

2,19,47; 2,21,51; 2,27,61; 2,28,65.67; 2,55,111; 2,80,157; etc.). The different mode of expression, for reasons of clarity or elegance, does not imply any detriment to the truth. On the other hand, the evangelists' conviction of the truth is so complete that it constitutes a criterion of interpretation. Any path that confirms that truth is valid; At the same time, the certainty that there can be neither lies nor falsities means that the investigation always remains open until a form of solution to the alleged contradictions is found, because such a solution exists. Ultimately, there is truth because it is the word of Truth. They are attributed to Christ, because they are true and he is the Truth (2,70,138). [17] «Res». The term res appears frequently in the work, but without being univocal. Its meanings are multiple. 1) Firstly, the generic sense of -subject- in question appears (2,12,29; 2,16,33; 2,27,63; 2,39,86; 2,50,105; 2,62,121). 2) We also encounter the meaning of any reality that can be the object of knowledge, both at the level of objects, actions or ideas (2,12,28; 2,21,51; 2,28,67). We translate by the generic -thing- or -something. 3) With explicit reference to the gospels, sometimes res simply indicates any specific event, fact or saying, narrated by the evangelist (2,21,52; 2,29,67; 2,49,103; 2,78,153; 3,4,13; 3,13,40; 3,25,70; 4,9,10); very frequently it is designated as res gesta (2,30,70; 2,34,81; 2,36,83; 2,40,87; 2,41,88; 2,43,91). We translate by -event-, -fact-. 4) In a new meaning it is identified with what modern exegetes call -narrative material-. In this case it is opposed to sententia, what Jesus said, that is, he dictates them according to another terminology (2,12,28; 2,19,47; 2,46,95.97). We translate it as -facts-. 5) In numerous cases it indicates the semantic content of the language, given by the author, both in proper and figurative use (1,22,30; 2,12,28; 2,19,29; 2,66,128; 3,7,30.31). We translate it as -content- or -meaning-. An author can use language in its own sense or in a figurative sense, and the res is nothing more than what he wanted to indicate with each term. In this sense res is contrasted with verba and locutions. Words do not exist except at the service of said res and, consequently, it must be preferred to those who make it known.

Furthermore, he says, if it were possible to know the carcass without their help, we could do without them. The truth must be sought more in the beef than in the verba (2,12,28). We are faced with a term that is fundamentally literary, but also exegetical. [18] Inspiration. That everything related to the gospels is regulated by God, through his Holy Spirit, is something about which Augustine has no doubt. If the evangelists have written their gospels, it is due to an order from the Lord (divinitus ordinatum: 1,2,3; imperavit: 1,35,54); If two of them were apostles and two others were not, it is also the work of divine Providence, through that same Spirit (1,1,2). But its divine action is much more extensive and profound; It is not exhausted in the order of writing or in the choice of authors. He goes so far as to intervene in themselves, in the powers that enable action for those who were elected, in the selection of the res, but not in that of S.Ag.

the words through which they are expressed, and even in more external aspects such as the ordo. The terminology that Augustine uses to designate this divine action on an author is varied. When this action takes place in a context outside the sacred books, it speaks of a movement of minds through an arcanus or occultus instinctus (1, 3, 5; 2, 70, 137). To refer to the sacred authors he uses the consecrated term of -inspiration-, both in the noun form (3, 13, 48) and in the verbal form (1, 2, 4). In one case he uses the stronger term dictare (1, 35, 54), and in others the biblical suggerere (2, 19, 44; 2, 21, 51; 3, 13, 48). But normally he prefers to use explanatory periphrases, among which the verb gubernareoregere stands out. The object of said verb are the minds (2, 21, 52; 3, 7, 30), the recordatio (3, 7, 30; 3,13,48) and the cor (3, 13, 48); He also speaks of a permissio or rather praeceptum coming from the authority of the Holy Spirit (3, 7, 31; 2, 21, 52), or of a constitutio (3,7,30). Leaving aside what refers to the occultus instinctus, because it does not apply to the evangelists, if we examine the data more closely, we notice that the divine work in the hagiographer is in no way to be understood as revelation, although a text in which it presents Jesus Christ as head as the source of the knowledge of the evangelists, its members, can be interpreted in that sense. In the phrase dictante capite cognoverunt, the verb dictare probably has to be given the strong meaning of •dictate-, according to the image it uses, which makes one think of the amanuensis: the hand that meekly follows the dictation of another, the head (1, 35, 54). The hand here would be only a means. In any case, what the text directly intends is to show the union between Christ and the evangelists, to be able to affirm that Christ wrote something, rather than defining the concept of "inspiration". Saving the previous text, divine action, as Augustine presents it, is exercised fundamentally on memory, which refers to things already known, although forgotten (ante cognita: 2,19,44; res cognitas: 2, 21, 51). In fact, if we review the previous terminology, we see that one of the terms most frequently used to express divine action is suggerere, a term with which the Vulgate translates the ypomnesei of Jn 14:26.

All the presences of said verb in this work of Augustine that have God as their subject are linked to the fact of remembering (sicut divinitus suggerebantur quae ante cognita postea remembering conscriberent: 2, 19, 44; quod voluisset Deus... eius recollectioni suggerere: 2, 21, 51; quo loco inspiratione divina suggestum est. Recordationes enim eorum...: 3, 13, 48). Furthermore, in the last text cited the divine inspiration has the effect of suggerere. And the verb inspirare itself has as its implicit object remembering (non tamen... velut alterius praecedentis ignarus... vel ignorála praetermisisse,... sed sicut unicuique inspiratum est: 1,2,4). Regarding the other actions attributed to God, the gubernare or regere, we already saw how one of the objects was precisely the memoria; but even when the object is the mens, it is so in relation to the memory (mentes... sanctorum... in recolendo quae scriberent sine dubio gubernans et regens: 2,21,52; mentes... gubernatae? Potuit enim ut animo Matthaei... occurreret: 3, 7, 30). Even when it comes to the cor it is not just any one, but the corda reminiscentium (3,13,48).

The same is said regarding the constitutio (non frustrating occurrisse aliudpro alio nomen prophetae, nisi quia ita Deus hoc scribi constituit: 3, 7, 30). From here, we can conclude that fundamentally the divine action on the hagiographer consists of the control of memories, in the active sense: that is, God makes the evangelist remember one thing or another or that he remembers it at a certain moment and not at another, and all this with a specific intention. Given that God is behind everything written, it must be affirmed that everything is "inspired"; but the "everything" refers to the res, not to the expression thereof. Against those who drew excessive conclusions from the action of God in man, Augustine explicitly dissociates the Holy Spirit from the genus, ordo and numerus of the words (2, 12, 28). In no way should it be thought that God is directly responsible for each of the words in their materiality. On the contrary, the Saint clearly indicates that we should not give them a quasi-magical value (consecratis sonis). God gives us the value of the content (res), not the words that exist in terms of it (2, 66, 128). to a certain extent of the ordo (we now leave aside the ordo verborum), in that by governing the memories it makes them appear at a certain moment in the story and not at another, with a precise intention (2, 21, 52; 3, 13, 48). of the divine persons does Augustine attribute that action to the sacred author? Since it is not a systematic study of it, he sometimes lacks the precision that we would like. Sometimes, he says nothing about it (1, 2, 4). 28; 3,7,30; 3, 13, 48).

Although it is a work of God, it is specifically a work of his providence (1, 1, 2; 3,7,30) or his power (2, 12, 28; 2, 70, 137; 3, 13, 48). God, through his Spirit, not only acts on the good, but also on the bad. With reference to them, it is not only worth noting the term instinctu, which in our work never refers to hagiographers, but also the adjective occultus. In effect, Augustine insists on the awareness that sacred authors have of God's action on them, parallel to the unconsciousness of others. The Truth speaks in each other, "either without knowing it, if they were evil, as in the case of Caiphas 0n 11,50), or knowing it, understanding it and believing it" as in the case of the evangelists (2, 70, 136). All this is placed in the context of the idea of ​​the original participation of Platonic philosophy, by virtue of which where truth is said it is Christ who says it, because he is the Truth (2, 60, 137). But in the case of sacred authors there is something more. Not only did he know, but he even felt that his mind was governed by the Spirit (3, 7, 30). The holiness of man is what makes the differences: -God frequently speaks even through the

evil and without their knowing it, by a certain hidden inspiration, moving the mind of man not by the merits of his holiness, but by right of his own power" (2,70,137). The origin of truth is always the Lord, but in some it produces scientia and sensus, and in others it does not. The consequence of the action of the Spirit is none other than concord (3,7,30) and the truth of the story (cf. complementary note 16: Truth). God's action is personal, not collective. The statement is explicit (unicuique inspiratum est: 1,2,4). This is precisely proven by the discrepancy between the evangelists, and is also proven by the conception of it as an action on memory. There is no collective memory, but individual memories. God's action is undeniable. But it is equally undeniable that the author does not stop acting as a man. In other words, he does not lose his personal freedom as a human author. For now, Augustine refers numerous times to the evangelist's intentio, that is, to what the author, personally, proposes with his writing (1,3,6; 1,5,8; 1,6,9, etc.). Frequently, in addition, this will of the sacred author is made explicit (1,6,9; 2,14,31). Regarding the words, there is no doubt. We already indicated how Augustine disconnects the Spirit from its genus, ordo and numerus. Each author looks for something with his story, and chooses the words based on what he is looking for (2,28,66). As for the ordo, the author at least has the freedom to put what God suggests to him; Submission to that known will of the Lord in no way annuls that freedom (2,21,51). Regarding res, he also enjoys freedom and is responsible for what he writes. In the case of the resurrection of Jairus' daughter, one author puts what Jairus said, another what Jairus wanted and thought (2,28,66). From among the material available to them, each person chose what they thought needed to be remembered (3,6,21), or what they considered to be sufficient (3,8,35), depending, in both cases, on its suitability or congruence with what they intended (4,8,9). In this way each evangelist made a personal contribution. Cf. VOGELS, St. Augustin Schrifts, 64-81; C. BASEVI, San Agustín. The interpretation of the New Testament. Exegetical criteria proposed by St. Augustine in the "De doctrina christiana", in the "Contra Faustum" and in the "De consensu evangelistarum" (Pamplona 1977). [19] Assimilation and disassimilation of facts.

When a narratio or locus, in the language of Augustine, or a pericope, in the language of modern exegetes, appears in two or more evangelists in similar, but not identical, terms, before admitting that one of them betrays the truth, Augustine offers several possibilities that make said truth compatible with the different formulations. One is to admit that the Lord said or did the same thing on more than one occasion or places (cf. supplementary note 24: Repeated data); another, that it is the same reality, but with the particularity that each evangelist provides complementary data (cf. complementary note 25: Supplementary data); another, that it is exactly the same fact or sentence, but with different formulations, or that it is about different facts or sentences, that is, that both took place. We can designate these last two cases, respectively, as
Additional notes

assimilation or dissimilation. Assimilation is very common, especially, but not exclusively, with reference to sentences that do not change even if their formulation changes for different reasons, among which is clarity (cf. supplementary note 14: "Sententia"). This is Agustín's preferred option and he resorts to it whenever force majeure arguments do not prevent him from following that path. When this is not viable, he opts for the principle we call disassimilation: Jesus said or did one and the other. By denying that they refer to the same thing, they cannot be accused of contradiction.

This procedure is used in the comparison of the following texts among others: Mt 3,11b with Me 1,7b (words of John the Baptist about Jesus) (2,12,29); Le 3,22c with Mt 3,17b and Mark 1,11b (the voice from heaven in the baptism of the Lord) (2, l4,31); Jn 1,35-44 with Mt 4,19, Mark 1,17 and Luke 5,10b (call of the first disciples) (2,17,37); Mt 4,18.21 and Me 1,16.19 (two by two, separately) with Le 5,10 (together) (2,17,41); Mt 4,12 (retreats to Galilee after John is delivered) with Jn 1,43 (retreats before John is delivered) and Le 4,13 (retires after baptism) (2,18,42); Mt 5, lss (sermon on the mountain) and Lk6,20bss (on the plain) (2,198,45); Me 5.11 (next to the mountain) and Le 3.32 (on the mountain) (2.24.56); Mt 9,2c and Me 2,5b (son) with Le 5,20b (man) (2,25,57); Mt 10,10 and Le 9,3 (no staff) with Me 6,8 (only staff) (2,30,71); Mt 12,9-13 (question of the Lord) with Me 3,1-6 and Le 6,6-11 (question of the Lord) (2,35,82); Jn 6,5b (Jesus asks Philip) with Mt 14,15b, Mark 6,35 and Luke 9,12 (the disciples ask Jesus) (2,46,96); Jn 6,15b (Jesus fled) with Mt 14,23 and Mark 6,46 (he withdrew to pray) (2,47,100); Mt 14,36 and Mc 6,56 (Jesus healed) with 6,22ff (spoke) (2,48,102); Mt 15,21 (walking) with Me 7,24b (at home) (2,49,103); Mt 19,17 (about the good) with Le 18,18 (you call me good) (2,63,123); Mt 26,52b (order not to use the sword) with Le 22,51a (limit to the use of the sword) (3,5,17), but introduces the distinction between the words and the fact to which they refer, stating that it could not be said with a blow what could be done with a blow (3,5,17); Jn 18,28b-30 (does not provide crimes) with Le 23,2 (provides them), finding the explanation in the fact that a selection took place among the abundant material of replies and counterreplies (3,8,35); Mt 27,54 and Me 15,39 (he was the Son of God) with Le 23,47 (he was righteous) (3,20,57); Mt 27, 59-60, Mark 15,46 and Luke 23,53 (Joseph, on a sheet) with Jn 19,39-42 (Joseph and Nicodemus, on two sheets) (3,26,60); Mt 28,2 (an angel) with Le 24,4 (two men in resplendent clothes) (3,24,67). In short, Augustine starts from the principle that the evangelists selected what seemed appropriate to them from the extensive material on Jesus. Some one thing, others another, sometimes very close to each other, but that, for that very reason, does not require identity, and consequently it cannot be said that they contradict each other when they do not fully coincide.

This is how Augustine formulates the principle on a theoretical level: - As it sometimes turns out that the Lord did something that seems to contradict another evangelist in something, without seeing a possible solution, it is not understood other than that both things were done and that each evangelist remembered one» (2,50,104). [20] "Voluntas." In Augustine's effort to show that there is no contradiction between the gospels, one of the concepts he resorts to is that of the voluntas. The resource, on the other hand, is not

invention of his personal genius; Without a doubt he only applies to the specific case what was prescribed in the manuals that he studied and had to comment on in his teaching activity. One of the regulae (cf. supplementary note 11: “Regulae”) mentioned by him insists that the voluntas of both the Lord, who spoke, and the evangelists who related what he had spoken, be considered. Knowing what Jesus had wanted to say, one can know whether the evangelists all served the truth in the diversity of expression of the words of the Lord that they offer. On the other hand, knowing what the evangelists intended when relating something or in a certain way, one can see if said contradiction exists or not. As I said before, this procedure fits perfectly into his previous training. We can place it within the criteria for the interpretation of legal texts, specifically in the quaestio de scripti et voluntatis, which arises in the case of leges contrae whose harmonization is achieved through recourse to the will of the legislator (QUINT., Instit. Orat. 7,5,5; 7,8,7; 3, 6, 43). This way of understanding would have a place in the work if we consider that Augustine begins it by indicating that Matthew focuses on the royal function of Christ, by which he rules and governs all men (l, 3, 5 ff). From that perspective, there is nothing strange that in some cases he applies it to his words, conceived as legal norms. The evangelists have given less importance to the vox (id., 7,5,6; 7,6,9) than to the voluntas of the Lord. But this is best placed on the purely literary level. -The interpretation of literary texts knows similar conditions: the text is interpreted by the philologist according to the voluntas auctoris. In the identity of the voluntas that the critic discovers when applying the norm of the literary ars, all divergence is annulled, even if it appears at the level of the verba (H. LAUSBERG, Manual, ni 15, 204, 209-210). Indeed, in the sophistic tradition any human literary composition could have solely aesthetic purposes; In the philosophical tradition, however, in which Augustine undoubtedly places these compositions (cf. De doctrina christiana I-II on the res of Scripture), although they take into account aesthetic motives with a view to better achieving what they intend, they do not exhaust themselves in delight for delight's sake.

The author has a voluntas at whose service are words, locutions and any literary artifice. Augustine moves in this tradition. If words are at the service of something, it is that something that must be sought, not stopped at them. This criterion of interpretation is considered by Augustine as res utilissimaypernecessaria (2, 28, 67), and he formulates it clearly and repeatedly. It is above all a criterion for the narrator: to only try to show the will, the intention of the subject, when he relates something about someone, regardless of whether it is a man, an angel or God (2, 46, 97). At the same time it is a reading criterion: in the words of a subject one should not look or search (inspicere - quaerere) for anything other than the will, since the words have no other reason for being than to be at the service of that will, of what they intend to communicate. Consequently, it is not possible to speak of a lie in the fact that someone expresses the will of another with words different from those he pronounced (2, 28, 67; 2, 46, 97; 2, 62, 121). The divergence in words or in the ordo narrandi

(2, 62, 121) does not mean betraying that will. What is said about words applies in the same way to the other signs with which the soul expresses itself (2, 28, 67). For Augustine it is not a principle obtained from worldly wisdom, but deduced from the behavior of the evangelists themselves. That is, the fact that we find in them a variety of expressions along with the concord in the res and sententiae (2, 46, 97). It is a conclusion that he draws from the concordant diversity of the four evangelists, which reveals to us that there is no lie if someone narrates something in a different way, but without departing from the will of the one with whom we must be in harmony and agreement (2, 66, 128). Principle that is the bearer of salvation for man (salubriter nosdoceri) (2, 46, 97). As in the entire work, this principle is not formulated by Augustine at the outset, but a posteriori, in the context of specific cases, to justify his harmonizing behavior. He resorts to it on several occasions: as a possibility, to harmonize Mt 3,1 I b (wearing his shoes) and Mc 1,7/Lk 3, l 6 b / J n 1,27 (untying the strap of his shoes), admitted that John did not intend anything other than to point out the excellence of the Lord and his own humility, an objective that is achieved with both formulations (2, 12, 29). The divergence between Mt 9,18d (dead) and M c 5,23b/Lk 8, 42 b (in the latter) finds a way of solution in the consideration of the will. An evangelist did not pay attention to the father's words about his daughter, but, more importantly (potissimum), to his will, and put down the words that declared that will. The difference between Mark and Luke, on the one hand, and Matthew, on the other, is that the former reflect what Jairus said and the latter what he wanted and thought (2, 28, 66). The discrepancy between Mt 19:7 (the Pharisees ask Jesus) and Mark 10:3 (Jesus asks) is unimportant - since both evangelists showed the intention of those who had spoken" (2, 62, 121). He also resorts to the same principle to explain the divergence in the dialogue between Jesus and the apostles in the context of the multiplication of the loaves (2, 46, 97), and, after a reasoning that is not easy to follow, to harmonize Matthew and Mark on the question of divorce (2, 62, 121); also regarding the spilling of the precious perfume in Bethany (2, 79, 156).

Jesus' intention to show how he unites Jews and Gentiles within himself justifies and makes credible that he pronounced the two words "Abba" and "Father" of Mark 14:36, contrary to what is indicated by Mt 26:39b/Lk 22, 42 (3, 4, 14). The serious divergence regarding the time of the crucifixion (according to Mark 15:25, at the third hour, and according to Jn 19, 1416 a, almost at the sixth hour) finds a solution by resorting to the will of the evangelist Mark, who wanted to indicate the Jews as morally responsible for the death of Jesus, while John indicates the material authors (3,13,46). In another order of things, the same divergence between the Hebrew text and the translation of the Septuagint finds no more probable explanation than this: although some expressions vary, they do not depart from the same will of God, from whom those sayings came and to whom the words should serve (2, 66, 128). [21] Codices. In the grammaticus school of antiquity, recourse to codices was essential as there was no printing press to fix and standardize the text. Not even the best copyist was exempt from the

possibility of error. It was a necessary procedure in one of the stages, that of emendatio, of the praxis of the grammar teacher. In our work there are traces of that activity in the former grammar teacher, with the same characteristics as those described by H.I. Marrou, in his work Saint Augustin et la fin de la culture antique (Paris 1938), p.23 - Augustine's recourse to codices is not global to establish a text that is as secure as possible, but rather occasional based on specific cases, normally when they are a source of problems. It does not lack criteria of healthy textual criticism. Thus, for example, it maintains the authenticity of the reading of Mt 27,8 per prophetam Hieremiam of some codices, instead of the simpler per prophetam of others, despite being against the truth, due to the criterion of difficult reading. In fact, he argues, it is easy to understand that someone, considering that the text attributed to Jeremiah was not his, deleted his name, while it is difficult to admit that someone added it, being as it is against historical truth. In short, the deletion is well explained, due to the difficulty it causes, and the addition is poorly explained. For this reason, then, the reading per prophetam Hieremiam must be accepted as authentic, even regardless of the fact that it is attested by the most ancient Greek codices (3,7,19). Once again he makes textual criticism regarding 1 Cor 15:5. If there are codices that instead of twelve disciples put eleven, it is because some men changed the figure by confusing the characters, believing that they were talking about the twelve apostles (then already eleven due to the death of Judas), when in reality they could be talking about other eleven disciples (3,25,71). It gives special value to the Greek codices, as well as to their antiquity (2,14,31; 3,7,29) and their number (3,7,29). But it is not an absolute criterion. In fact, it accepts any reading as long as it appears in a fide dignus codex, without further specifying what these are (2,14,31).

In reality, the variants of the codices do not seem to worry him; In fact, in our text he only rejects one as incomplete (the one mentioned above referring to Mt 27,8), doubts another and admits all the others, either because he sees them as complementary (2,14,31, regarding Luke 3,22; they add: ego hodie genui te), or because he considers them as linguistic idiotisms, which one translator maintains and another does not, when transferring it from Greek to Latin (2,28,68, a purpose of Mt 9,24; they put mulier instead of atpuella), either because they are considered alternatives (2,30,70, regarding Mt 10,3; they put Lebdeo instead of Thaddeus; 2,51,106, regarding Mt 15,39; they put Dalmanuta for Mageda), or because they are synonyms (4,2,3, regarding Mark 1,26; they put convexans instead of discerpens). If Mt 21:4, in its quotation from Zech 9:9, unlike the Church codices of the usual translation, speaks of an ass, the explanation is that this evangelist who wrote, according to tradition, in Hebrew, used Hebrew codices, and not those of the Greek translation of the Septuagint (2,66,128). Only in one case, as we indicated, regarding 1 Cor 15,5, does he doubt whether the correct reading is undecim or duodecim, given that both are possible depending on whether the eleven apostles or the other twelve disciples are referred to (3,25,71-, later, consulting the Greek text will dispel the doubt, cf.

Quaestiones in Heptateuchum 1,117: CSEL 28/2 59-60). But here the criterion is not strictly textual criticism, but of another order. In general, Augustine refuses to believe that any codex is mendacious, as long as he can find an explanation, even if it is theological, and not of a nature of pure textual criticism (3,7,29). Agustín prefers not to seek protection in the reading provided by the different codices to solve certain difficulties. If some codices read per prophetam Hieremiam, while others read simply per prophetam, given that the difficulty is caused precisely by the name, the Hieremiam, because it attributes to Jeremiah what belongs to Zechariah, he could save the situation by admitting as valid only the reading of the latter. But he prefers that of the former, for reasons of pure textual criticism, preferring to seek a theological explanation for the inclusion of Jeremiah by Zechariah (3,7,29). Our work allows us to notice that Augustine had several codices from Luke (2,14,31), from Matthew (2,28,68; 2,30,70; 2,51,106), from Mark (2,51,106; 4,2,3). In Augustine, also at the service of the explanatio (2,70,137). [22] -Narratio brevis et aperta». According to classical rhetoric, there are three virtues of narration (virtutes narrationis). In this regard, Cicero expresses himself this way: oportet igitur eam tres habere (virtutes): ut brevis, ut aperta, utprobabilis sit (De inventione 1,20,28; cf. also Tópica 26,91; Rhetorica ad Herennium 1,9,14; QUINT., Instit. Orat. 4,2,31 with slightly different formulations and order). That is, the perfect narrative must have brevity, clarity and verisimilitude, although the order varies among different authors. The supreme goal it pursues is to engender in the public the conviction of the veracity of the narrative through verisimilitude. The other two virtues, brevity and clarity, are means to achieve verisimilitude that persuades of truthfulness. Clarity is ordered to understanding, to cognitio, while brevity can be either at the service of attentum or docilem parare, or at the service of memory. Depending on the circumstances, preference should be given to the narratio brevis or the narratio aperta. On narrationis virtutes in general and specifically, cf, H. LAUSBERG, Manual, n.293-337. Augustine, who considers the gospels as narrationes (cf. complementary note 10: The gospels as -narratio"), could not help but evaluate them from the criterion of virtutes.

Furthermore, they are used to achieve the objective of the work, that is, to show harmony between everyone. The requirements of the narratio brevis, in some cases, and the narratio aperta, in others, explain divergences between the various evangelical stories; divergences that, in this context, are merely quantitative, never qualitative; That is, they do not mean any contradiction. Augustine goes even further and in the literary characterization of the evangelists he points out that Mark is dominated by the desire for a narratio brevis, while Luke is dominated by the desire for the narratio aperta. In this way, what in the eyes of the accusers may seem like proof of serious divergence between one evangelist and another, in the eyes of those who understand grammatical science is nothing more than submission to the rules of literary art. The accusation denotes both bad faith and ignorance.

Let's start with the brief. Augustine keeps in mind the purpose of the Gospel of John, according to which, if everything that Jesus did were written down, there would be no room for books in the world (n 21, 25). This means that all evangelists have had to follow criteria of brevity. But, within this, it is possible to establish a kind of hierarchy in this regard, which Augustine formulates in this way: "Let us think how briefly Mark said this in comparison to Matthew, how briefly Matthew compared to Luke, how briefly Luke compared to John and, finally, how briefly John compared to what happened" (3, 13. 47). The text refers to the passion of the Lord, but has application to all of the gospels. Regarding Mark, Augustine presents him as the breviator of Matthew (1,2,4; 2, 30, 70: 2, 76, 146), and also affirms of him that maxime brevitatis sectator est and explicitly indicates that in the evangelist this is a conscious fact (3, 13, 47), that for him it has become a custom to present his stories in abbreviated form (breviter perstringere) (3, 25, 75). If each evangelist expounded the Lord's sentences as he thought best, that is, brevius velprolixius (2,12,27). It is clear that Marcos was left with the first part of the alternative. It should not be forgotten that Augustine's objective is to show that the evangelists do not cancel each other, but that there is always room for agreement between them and that his considerations on the brevity, for now, of the evangelists are directed to this objective. Thus, for example, the difference between Mt 9,35-10,42 and Mark 6, 6 b - l l finds a possible explanation in terms of brevity, since it seems that Mark condensed that passage into a few words (hunc locum breviter videtur perstrinxisse) (2, 30, 70). Concern for brevity even provokes the alteration of the ordo by Mark, who placed before Matthew the reason why divorce was allowed for reasons of brevity (brevitatis causa) (2, 66, 122). If according to Mark 10:35 it was the sons of Zebedee who personally said what according to Mt 20:20 their mother said, presenting their will, it was demands for brevity that prompted Mark to silence the mediator of the supplication. Obviously brevity of concepts rather than words (2, 64, 124). Me 15:14 is also separated from Mt 27:23-25 ​​for reasons of brevity.

He wanted to concisely indicate Pilate's will and his efforts for the life of the Lord. With the question that he puts in Pilate's mouth: What evil has he done? (Me 15,14) he briefly hinted at what had taken place in a longer period of time, but always attentive to being understood. In fact, remembering what he wanted to be understood, he did not say "said", but "said". The appropriate use of the tenses of the verb serves in a special way to clearly express what is meant (3, 13, 47). While Le (24, 13-35) offers the complete account of the appearance to the disciples of Emmaus, Mark gives it in summary (breviter perstringit) (3, 25, 71. 75). Me 3,16 refers to the same thing as Jn 1,42, but abbreviated (4,3,4). To such an extent does Augustine associate Mark, on a literary level, with the narratio brevis, that he can make a statement based on the sole reason that, otherwise, Mark would be caught putting something superfluous in the mouth of the Lord (3, 2, 7). In the narration of the Gethsemane scene Augustine compares Mark
