with Matthew and perceives in him the combination of the two demands: brevity and clarity, depending on the case (aliquanto brevius quasdam constringens sententias et aliquid magis aperiens) (3,4,11). In the invitation to beware of the Pharisees and their hypocrisy that both Matthew (23,1-36) and Mark (12, 37 b - 40) refer to, Augustine perceives two contrasting literary criteria: while the first resorts to abundance (latissime... copied digessit), the second, as is his custom, prefers to stick to brevity (breviterperstrinxit) (2,76,146). But in numerous other cases Mark and Matthew are associated, compared to Luke, in the narratio brevis. Regarding the call of the first disciples, Matthew (4, 18-22) and Mark (1,16-20) breviterperstringunt what Luke (5,1-11) apertius explicavit (2, 17, 37). In the passion story, reasons of brevity lead both Matthew and Mark to silence Peter's return to the court (3, 6, 24); In the same way, to summarize (compendium) they put the plural for the singular (3, 6, 25); together they also allow themselves to be guided by reasons of brevity in the scene of false witnesses (3, 7, 27). The divergence between Mt 27,44 and Mc 15,32b, on the one hand, and Luke 23, 39-43, on the other, referring to the thieves who insulted him, is only literary, since Matthew and Mark gave an abbreviated version of the events (breviterperstringentes) (3,16,53). But Mateo also knows how to go only in the demands of brevity. Here are some examples: Mt 8,5 (a centurion) cannot be considered in contradiction with Le 7,3 (some elders of the Jews) because Matthew in that circumstance resorted to the compendium, brevity taken to the extreme (QUINT., Inst. Orat. 4, 2, 46), which prompted him to silence that said centurion had arrived through other people (2, 20, 49). This is not the only case in which Augustine attributes Matthew to having resorted to the compendium. The expression ad quemdam of 26, 18 was introduced by him on his own initiative (ex persona sua) out of a desire for brevity (studio brevitatis illum compendio voluit insinuare), believing (illi videretur) that such a compendium did not harm clarity (cum hoc illi ad insinuandam iubentis sententiam sufficere videretur), although that is not the opinion of the literary critic, who sees it as a subobscura locutio for demands of brevity (necessitate brevitatis) (2,80,157).

If in the account of the resurrection of Jairus' daughter according to Matthew (9:18 d) the daughter has already died, while in Mark (5:23) and Luke (8:42) she is still on her last legs, - so that no contradiction appears we must... understand that for reasons of brevity (brevitatis causa), Matthew meant rather that he prayed to the Lord to do what he actually did... Matthew, meaning to say it (cum instituisset... dicere) all briefly, indicated that the father in his supplication said what is true that he wanted and Christ did" (2, 28, 66). The difference between Luke 20,9a and Mt 21,33a is explained because Matthew was silent for reasons of brevity (brevitatis causa) what Luke did not omit (2,70,137). Luke also condescends from time to time to the demands of narratio brevis. In Luke 9:1-6 he imitates the brevity of Mark (2, 30, 70). Other times it even surpasses him; This is the case of Luke 9:13b, where Luke summarizes in a single sentence the response of Philip and that of Andrew (Jn 6:7-9) (2, 46, 96). John stands out not precisely for his brevitas, but for his prolixitas (4, 10, 15, 18) and diuturnitas (4,10,19).

Regarding narratio aperta, we must begin with general statements. The different formulation of some of the Lord's sentences by the evangelists is not something capricious or pure literary aesthetics, but is at the service of a better understanding of them (altos ad eandem sententiam familiarius explicandam verba variousse, ut intellegatur...) (2,14,31); or in other words, »the sentence is all the better expressed because, although certain words have changed, the truth has remained (both melius insinuata quanto quibusdam verbis... variata) (2,27,61). Leaving aside these general formulations, if we go into each specific evangelist, the center shifts to Luke; It is he, according to Augustine, who most systematically provides clarity with his story. These are the examples: Le 5,32-35 clarifies (evidentius expressit) Me 2,18-20 indicating the same (2,27,62); specifically, Le 5:34 clarifies and elegantly (eleganter aperuit) Mark 2:29 (2,27,63); in the scene of the centurion's servant Luke clarified (aperuit) how everything had developed, so that we would be forced to understand (ut ex hoc intellegere cogeremur) from there why he said that someone who could not lie had accessed him (2,20,50); The word man (Luke 5:20), instead of son, serves to better explain the Lord's sentence (ad sententiam domini expressius insinuandam valet) (2:25,57); The same is said of the addition of in poenitentiam of Luke 5,32 (ad explanandam sententiam valet) (2,27,61); Le 6,6-11 clarifies for us (aperuisset) that the scene took place on another Saturday and, therefore, is different from the one narrated by Mt 9,12-14 (2,35,82). Although it does not refer to what is indicated by Mt 24,20 or Mark 13,18, Le 21,34-36 illuminates the sentence (inlustrasse sententiam) provided by them (2,77,151); In the account of the scene in the garden of Gethsemane, Luke made it clearer (manifestius aperuit) to what distance Jesus had retreated (3,4,13); with his narration Luke explained (narrando explicavit) what Mark overlooked (Emmaus scene) (3,25,73). Marcos, normally characterized by brevity, also makes concessions to clarity. In the account of Peter's denial (14:30) he is distinguished from Matthew (26:34) by a greater contribution of details (distinctius). This distinctio is at the service of clarity (QUINT., Instit. Orat. 4,2,36: -erit... narratio aperta... si fuerit... distincta rebus, personis...••).

Of all the evangelists it is he who planius elocutus est, who narrated it expressius (3,2,7). Likewise in the interrogation of Jesus by the high priests, Mark's presentation provides more clarity in that Mark 14:62 eliminates the ambiguity of Mt 26:64: tu dixisti (3:6,20). [23] «Praeoccupatio-Recapitulatio». The narratio of the different evangelists does not maintain the same order, which some interpret as proof of contradiction between them. Augustine does not think so, who repeatedly affirms that the different ordo in no way affects the truth of the gospels or their harmony (cf. complementary note 6: "Ordo"). The divergence in the ordo can be the result of a digression, for example. In this case one cannot properly speak of a broken ordo, since there is nothing more than the introduction of a new element in the set of other common ones. This break occurs when the same narrative elements are placed in different places, fitting two

possibilities: that an element is placed before or after the place where it belongs according to the ordo rerum. The first case Augustine designates with the verb recapitulare or the noun recapitulatio, and the second with the verb praeoecupare. Both terms refer to rhetorical figures. With the term praeoecupare/praeoecupatio Augustine refers to prolepsis. He states this explicitly in Quaestiones in Heptateuchum. Referring to a question raised by the Exodus, he affirms that he finds a solution by noting the existence of prolepsis: per prolepsin, hoc est, perpraeoecupationem anticipat Scriptura quodpostea factum est (2,103; cf. also 7,3.10.11.12; on prolepsis, cf. H. LAUSBERG, Manual, n.855). In turn, with the term recapitulare/recapitulatio Augustine alludes to the figure of recapitulatio, in Greek anacephalaiosis, as he also refers to it explicitly in Quaestiones in Heptateuchum: aut hic per anacephalaiosin dicitur aut illie per prolepsin dictum est, id est, aut hic recapitulando aut illie praeoecupando (7,10; on recapitulatio or anacephalaiosis, cf. H. LAUSBERG, Manual, n.434-435, 671). The use of this figure to solve biblical questions is abundant. In the same work we write down the following: 1,12.20.25.53.55, 75,87,107,118,128,155; 2,44,154; 4.30; 7.3; Locutions in Heptateuchum 1,132,188. The recapitulatio corresponds to the sixth rule established by Tyconius. Thus Augustine writes in De doctrina christiana: «Tyconius designates as "Recapitulation" the sixth rule that a very attentive study of the scriptures led him to discover- (3,36,52). And he describes it in the following way: -In effect, certain events are referred to as if they were later in the order of time or related in the continuous plot of events, while the story, without appearing to do so, goes back to previous events that had been omitted» (id.). In Augustine's presentation they consist of breaking the ordo by narrating something at a time respectively after or before the one to which it corresponds. He describes it as remembering what had been overlooked (2,44,92; 3,9,36) or anticipating what would follow later in an authentic ordo rerum (2,19,44). Instead of recapitulare or praeoecupare, he sometimes uses the verbs revocare^ antecapere respectively (2,30,70). In Augustine's opinion, the four evangelists, without exception, frequently resort to recapitulatio.

He finds recapitulations in Mt 4,13: going to Capernaum and 4,19: I will make you fishers of men (2,17,39); 26,6-13: anointing in Bethany (2,78,153); Mt 27, 27ff: flagellation and crowning with thorns (3,9,36). Mark 14,3-9: anointing in Bethany (2,78,153); Mark 15,16ff: flagellation and crowning with thorns (3,9,36); Mark 15:25: third hour and crucifixion (3:13,42); Mt: Peter's denial (3,13,50); Me: Peter's denial (3,13,50); Mark 3,16: name Peter (4,3,4). Le 22,63-71: insults to Jesus (3,7,27); Le 23,46: voice, vinegar and death (3,19,56); Le 24,12: Peter in the tomb (3,25,70). Jn 6, l6ff: crossing the lake (2,47,100); Jn 18,25-27: Peter's denial (3,6,24). It should be noted that in several cases Matthew and Mark appear together in the recapitulatio. On the other hand, as regards the praeoecupatio, except for one occasion,

sion in which he attributes it to Matthew (Mt 27, 19: Pilate's wife) (3, 13, 46), the others he attributes to Luke, of whom he says that it is a custom (ut solet) (3, 1, 2). Here they are: Luke 8, 19-21: the relatives of Jesus (2, 40, 87); Le 4, l 6 s s: presence in Nazareth (2, 42, 90); Le 3,19-20: prison of John the Baptist (2, 44, 92); Le 23, 45: darkening of the sun and tearing of the veil of the temple (3, 16, 56); Le 13,34-35; threats against Jerusalem (2, 75, 145); Le 17,22-37; the day of the Son of man (2, 77, 151); Le 22, 15-18: first mention of the cup (3, 1, 2). With respect to both the recapitulatio and the praeoecupatio, we must remember what was said regarding the ordo in general, namely: that it has no importance in itself in relation to the truth, as long as it does not mean an internal contradiction or with reference to the other evangelists, among other things because the memory of whom it depends is regulated by God, like the ordo in general (2, 21, 51) (cf. complementary note 6: «Ordo-). By giving this explanation of the divergences in the ordo, Augustine, once again, wants to show how the difficulties have their solution without leaving the literary field. In fact, he explicitly places the recapitulatio in that context by comparing it with the praxis of the orators: -as it is customary in a speech to return in a certain way to something already omitted- (2, 47, 100). It is worth noting, however, a small difference. The recapitulatio or praeoecupatio of the speaker is the result of free choice, for aesthetic reasons or as a requirement of the narratio brevis. On the other hand, the recapitulatio and praeoecupatio of the evangelists, as presented by Augustine, is normally not their personal choice, but rather a simple mechanical result of the functioning of memory, which does not function in a programmed way, but often ex occasione (2, 44, 92), or by gift, obviously from God. In this context, the most that can be achieved is to place that choice on God, given that it is he who governs and governs the memory of the evangelist (cf. complementary note 15; Memory and 18: Inspiration). In this case, it would be God, rather than the evangelist, who would be responsible in this regard.

However, Augustine mentions a case referring to the recapitulatio, and another to the praeoecupatio in which it appears as consciously sought by the evangelist: I refer to Mark 15, 25, for the first. The introduction by Mark, Augustine thinks, of that text as a recapitulatio serves a special purpose of the author: to mean something that only those who search for it will find; specifically, to show who were truly responsible for the death of Jesus (3, 13, 42). Similarly, the praeoecupatio represented by Luke 4:17ff is not fortuitous, but conscious; For Augustine it is evident from the fact that he mentions things that he knows very well that he has not narrated; In that context, there is no room for forgetting (2, 42, 90). Noting whether such a recapitulatio exists or not is the result of careful consideration of the text, specifically of the transitus from one period to another. Special attention deserves the chronological references in them (2, 17, 39; 2, 78, 153), or the lack of any connection with what came before and what came after (2, 40, 87). The comparison with another evangelist who perhaps clearly points out the ordo rerum is of great value in this regard (2, 42, 92). However, certainty is not always obtained (2, 17, 39). Furthermore, sometimes you get the certainty that something is placed outside the order, but

It is difficult to delimit whether it is a recapitulare or a praeoecupare (2, 19, 44; 2,23,54; 2,30,70; 2,47,100; 3,2,5; Quaest. in Hept. 7, 310. 11). The problem is reduced, therefore, to knowing which evangelist, in a given case, follows the ordo rerum and which only the ordo remembranceis (2,30,70). In short, Augustine means, a literary sensitivity that allows us to capture the stylistic resources, in this case the prolepsis and anacephalaiosis that the sacred authors have used, will dispel doubts about the veracity of their stories. [24] Repeated data. When a fact or sentence is reported by two evangelists in an almost identical or at least similar way, but identification is not possible, before denying the truth of the Gospel story, another solution must be accepted: the fact or sentence was carried out or pronounced by the Lord on more than one occasion. Augustine tends to constitute specific cases as a general rule. Thus, for example, from the fact that according to Matthew Jesus is asked twice for a sign from heaven (Mt 16:1-4 and 12:38-39), he concludes that the Lord said the same things on more than one occasion, and then extracts the general principle: "so that, in the case of a contradiction that cannot be resolved, it is understood that he said it twice" (2, 51, 106). He draws the same conclusion regarding Mt 16:19 and Mt 18:18 (power to bind and loose). He argues this way: -in order not to have to always repeat it, we must remember, as I have already stressed repeatedly, that Jesus said the same things frequently and in many places. Let us never be troubled if some think that the order of his words contradicts one another (2, 61, 119). It does not occur to Augustine to think about the other possibility, namely, that the evangelist could have put the same information on more than one occasion, despite the fact that repetitio was contemplated in the rhetorical norms. Augustine resorts to this solution at least on several occasions. It is the one offered to avoid the contradiction between Mt l l, 20-24 and L c 10,13-15 (rebuke to the cities of Galilee) (2, 32, 79); between Mt 12:38-45 and Le 11:16-32 (sign of Jonas and conflict with Satan) (2, 39, 86); between Jn 2:13-16, on the one hand, and Mt 12, 13, Mell, 11.

15-17 and Le 19, 45-46, on the other (purification of the temple) (2, 67, 129); between Le 10,25-28 and Me 12,28-31 (the main commandment) (2, 73, 142); between Mt 24, 20 and Mark 13,18, on the one hand, and Le 21,34-36, on the other (need to be awake) (2, 77, 151); between Mt 26, 30-33, Jn 13,33-38, Mark 14,26-31 and Le 22,31-34 (announcement of the denial) (3, 2, 5), and between Mark 16,14 and Jn 20,19-25 (appearance of Jesus) (3, 25, 76). To tell the truth, Agustín is not enthusiastic about the procedure judging by his use of it. For now, he usually presents it as a second alternative to another that does not clear up all doubts (2, 77, 151; 3, 25, 76). The difficulty of maintaining the veracity of the story in any other way forces him (cogant) to accept that solution as the most probable (3, 25, 76). The difficulty of harmonization that prevents us from affirming that it is the same fact always comes from the different order, that is, from the place where they are placed. Although it is true that Augustine relativizes this ordo as far as the truth of the story is concerned, sometimes it cannot be ignored, since in both cases it is about the ordo rerum. In some others, however, it is not only the ordo that

prevents identification and requires diversification, but rather the elements of the story themselves, such as the assessment it includes of the people involved (2,73,142). [25] Supplementary data. The principle repeated by Augustine that the evangelists are not complete either in the material they provide or in the way in which they present it, that is, that some remain silent about what others say, allows him an easy solution to certain divergences. Sometimes he encounters evangelical data to which he cannot apply criteria that are useful for other cases, such as admitting the diversity of expression with identical content, or considering them as different facts, since he is certain or has evidence that he is faced with the same event. For Augustine, the existence of this particular data that is divergent from another Gospel narrative in no way represents any problem that affects the truth of any of the stories. Its very truth and the necessary harmonization in no way contradict or require the cancellation of the other: both data are complementary. Let's look at examples of this harmonization method. The first refers to Mt 8:18 (he ordered them to go to the other shore) and Luke 9:57 (when they were on their way): the solution is to admit both, that is, that they were on their way to the other shore (2,23,54). He will only see opposition between Mark 8:27 (on the road) and Luke 9:18 (praying alone), he says, who has never prayed on the road (2,53,108). Complementary data are also those offered by Mt 26,7b and Mark 14,3d (the head), on the one hand, and jn 12,3b (the feet), on the other, regarding the place of Jesus' body on which Mary Magdalene poured her ointment (2,77,155). The same solution is offered to the divergence between Mt 27:54 (they felt fear) and Le 23:47 (they glorified God); There is no contradiction between the stories of both evangelists because those present glorified God with their fear (3,20,57). [26] Subject. Under this heading we refer to the activity of the critic who tries to decipher the subject of a statement. In fact, we frequently discover Augustine trying to decipher whether, when faced with some saying or sentence, the evangelist should be considered as an author or as a simple narrator. And, even more so, in the case that he is simply a narrator, to whom the authorship must be attributed properly.

It is a grammatical exercise to elucidate who vox is a certain statement, that is, to whom what is related must be attributed (quae verba quibus sint tribuenda personis: 2,70,138). The aspects that we find in the Saint's behavior are diverse. In some cases he tries to find out who the grammatical subject is; in others, to discover the real subject, if it happens, not infrequently, that it is distinguished from the grammatical one; In others, finally, your task will be to decipher the number of subjects, or who the recipients of the words are. We find that sometimes Augustine stops to establish the distinction between what comes ex persona Domini and what comes ex persona sua, that is, from the initiative of the evangelist. In some cases, in fact, it is not clear. This is the case with Mt 3:3, where it is doubtful (ambigue) whether Matthew continues quoting words from John or introduces them personally (utrum ex persona sua Matthaeus boc commemoraverit). In one case Augustine refers that both Mt 11,21-23 and Le

10,13-14 present Jesus' words in direct style (ex ipsius ore) (2,32,79). Ex persona sua (of the evangelist) are, referring to Mark, Mark 14,1; to Luke, Le 22,1 (2,78,152). The expression ad quemdam (Mt 26,18) is inserted by Matthew ex persona sua... non ex Domini persona (2,80,157). Also on his own initiative (expersona ipsius evangelistae), Matthew introduces, under the name Jeremiah, something that is neither his nor Zechariah's (Mt 27,9-10) with a deep meaning (mystice) (3,7,31). Considering the distinction between the grammatical subject and the real subject is for Augustine a source of solutions. In this context he speaks of certain locutions of Scripture. Among them is one in which the sacred author usually speaks about himself in the third person; This is not an isolated case, but rather a frequent one. Augustine does not lack examples that confirm his assertion: Mt 9,9; Jn 21,24; Mt 9,6; 16.27; 17.9; Me 8,31.38; Jn 5,25; Le 24,46 (cf. In lo. ev. 61,4 where he offers other examples). The fact allows him to overcome, specifically, the apparent divergence between Jn 1:23, in which John applies the text of Is 40:3 to himself, and the other evangelists, where John himself uses the third person (2,12,25). The same distinction between the grammatical subject and the real subject has other applications. In the scene of the healing of the centurion's son, there is a divergence in the grammatical subjects between Mt 8,5 (a centurion) and Le 7,3 (some elders of the Jews), but they coincide in the real subject, given that the elders represent the former. In fact, Matthew only used a habitual way of speaking (usitatus mos loquendi) that does not take into account the intermediary, and that he explains with examples (2,20,49). He also resorts to this representativeness to harmonize Mt 20,21 (the mother) and Mark 10,35 (her children) (2,64,124), and in a certain way Mt 26,73/Mc 14,70b (those who dealt with Peter) and Jn 18,26 (only one, to whom the others attest) (3,6,25). Along with the idea of ​​representativeness is that of moral unity, through which we can speak of a kind of collective subject. Christ and the disciples form such a solid unity that what is said to them or from them must be understood as being said to him or from him. This is how Augustine resolves the divergences between the evangelists on the famous question about fasting, specifically between Mt 9:11 b (Why does your Master eat...?) and Luke 5:30b (Why do you [the disciples] eat and drink?) (2,27,61).

For Augustine there is no room to speak of divergence by virtue of the intimate union between Christ and the disciples. But here he already works with criteria other than purely grammatical ones. He resorts to this type of identification, which allows us to affirm that the real subject is also Jesus when the grammatical subject is the disciples or vice versa, in other cases and under the protection of other assumptions of a more philosophical-theological nature. Starting from the fact that Jesus is the Truth and that his disciples told the truth, one can conclude in the non-contradiction in texts such as Mt 21:41 (they say Jesus), on the one hand, and Mark 12:9b and Luke 20:16 (he says [Jesus]), on the other. In fact, "this answer has been attributed to the Lord because, when (the disciples) said a truth, he himself answered it, which is the Truth, through their mouths" (2,70,134). The same argument, but this time on a purely theological basis, the unity in the mystical Body, serves to harmonize Mt

21, 41 (they say Jesus), on the one hand, and Mark 12, 9 and Luke 20, 16 (Jesus says), on the other. He comments: "They could have been such that, not without foundation, they were considered to already be members of the same body of the Lord, so that their voice (eorum vox Mi tribueretur) was precisely attributed to him of whom they were already members" (2, 70, 137). In other cases the roles are reversed, but from the same beginning. Thus he considers what appears in the mouth of Jesus as said by the Church (2, 75, 145). Here we see Augustine's effort to merge theological criteria into criteria of a grammatical nature, such as the identity of the real subject, despite the diversity of the grammatical subject. Augustine draws attention to another reality, namely, the existence of a multiplicity of subjects, to each of whom one of the partial aspects of the story that seems to be in contradiction can be attributed. This implies that the stories do not exhaust the details, but are fragmentary. Noting this gives reason, for example, for each evangelist to tell the truth despite the fact that they provide different comments from the apostles after the storm has calmed down (2, 24, 55). Discovering this multiplicity of subjects requires a certain effort. The comparison between the evangelists or the logic of the text itself allows us to discover who and about whom they said something. In this regard, Augustine presents a true grammatical analysis to determine the subject of the verbs "arrive- and "say-" of Mark 2:18, resulting in the fact that they say it alios de aliis, that is, of third parties, as confirmed by Luke 5:33. Consequently, if they are different subjects, the statements presented by Mt 9:14 and Mark 2:18 are different, and there is no room to speak of contradiction. Sometimes the subjects are implicit and discovering them means solving the difficulty. An implicit subject must be recognized, Augustine thinks, in jn 8,31-38 if he wants to avoid a contradiction arising between 8,31 (to those who had believed in him) and 8,33 (reply). attribute each statement- (2, 70, 138).

Starting from the fact that there are gaps in the stories of each evangelist, Augustine also tries to establish the correspondence between question and answer by mixing the different stories. In this way, linking a certain statement with a question referred by another evangelist, overcomes the difficulty. In essence, it has only established that there is a plurality of subjects to whom each of the statements must be assigned separately, thus avoiding the problem. This is what he does on the occasion of the divergences in the story about the multiplication of the loaves (2, 46, 96). He applies this same criterion to resolve the divergences between Mt 21, 41 (they say to Jesus) and Mark 12,9b/Lk 20, 16 (says [Jesus]): -it can be easily understood that... their words were introduced without inserting the "they said" or "they answered", but taking it as understood" (2, 70, 134). Augustine's procedure is not limited to determining the subject or subjects to whom to attribute a certain statement; He also extends it to find out the recipient of the same. The diversity of these makes certain texts intelligible, without the need to affirm that they contradict each other. Examples of this result from the comparison of Le 22, 51 b with Mt

26, 52 b regarding the scene of the sword in the garden of Gethsemane (2, 5, 15) and also to compare Mt 22, 42-45, on the one hand, and Mark 12, 35-37 a and Luke 20, 41-44, on the other, regarding the Davidic filiation of Christ (2, 74, 143). The conclusion is clear: The pure grammatical analysis of the text that determines the subject or subjects, or even the recipient of the words that seem in contradiction, leads to noticing that such a contradiction does not exist. But it must be noted that in the case of Augustine the prejudice of the veracity of the evangelical text is always ahead. A text provides clarity about its way of arguing: from the fact that the verb is plural it deduces that there were several subjects (3, 6, 24). Another critic without such prejudice would have considered the possibility of an incorrectness, a solecism or a figure, but not Agustín. [27] Synecdoche. The literary figure of synecdoche (cf. QUINT., Instit. Orat. 8,6,19; Rhetorica ad Herennium 4, 33, 44, which he calls intellectio; H. LAUSBERG, Manual, n. 572-577) offered Augustine considerable help in achieving the objective of the work. Out of fidelity, no doubt, to the eminently pastoral purpose that guides his writing and leads him to be understood by everyone, even the least educated, as happens in other parallel cases, he always avoids the specific name of synecdoche, sylepsis or antonomasia, as well as that of metonymy or "trope." This last indication is replaced with other generic formulations such as (usitatus) loquendi modus (2, 56, 113; 3, 24, 65. 66), locutio (2, 79, 156), locutio usitata (3, 6, 25), locutionis modus (3. 16, 53; 3, 24, 66), genus locutionis satis usitatum (3, 16, 53; 3, 17, 54) or, from a criterion that is no longer linguistic, but rather based on information about who resorts to them, quemadmodum loquiscripturaesolent (3, 13, 41), mos scripturarum (3,25,84). Although we do not find the term synecdoche in the work, we do find a vulgar definition of it: the known a parte totum, that is, the metonymy of quantitative relationship between the word used and the meaning mentioned (H. LAUSBERG, Manual, n. 572).

Augustine finds this quantitative relationship in different ways in which it can manifest itself: the simple relationship parts everything in both directions and in the numerical relationship, in addition to the case of antonomasia and the genus-species relationship. The first case is noticed by Augustine when he tries to resolve the divergence between Mark 6:40 and Luke 9:14b regarding the multiplication of the loaves; In this case it is Luke who resorts to synecdoche by indicating only a part (groups of fifty) for the whole (groups of fifty and one hundred). Indeed, unus partem dixit, alter totum (2, 46, 98). The resource also allows him to harmonize the stories of the transfiguration, that is, Mt 17,1/Mc 9,2 (six days later) and Le 9, 28 (about eight days later); here pars pro toto commemoratur (2, 56, 113). In 3,13,41 he goes to him to harmonize Mark 15,25 (third hour) and jn 19,14-16a (almost sixth); in 3, 24, 64, for the same with Mt 28,1a (on Saturday afternoon) and Mark 16,2/Lk 24,1/Jn 20,1 (very early in the morning/very early in the morning/at dawn), the same as in 3,24,66 for the triduum of the resurrection, which cannot be understood otherwise, or in 3,24,84 to give a special meaning to the spaces

temporary between the appearances of the Lord. See also the harmonization between Mark 14,13 (pitcher) and Luke 22, 10 (amphora), in 2, 80, 157. Synecdoche as a quantitative numerical relationship is also called syllepsis. Saint Jerome has no qualms about using the term in places where Augustine will offer the same solution (Commentarium in Matthaeutn: CC 77, 246, 1020 s; 273, 1739); Augustine, on the other hand, limits himself to describing it and affirming that the expression is used in Scripture. Within what occupies his attention in this work, he detects the recourse to syllepsis by the evangelists in the following places: in 2, 46, 96 as a possibility of harmonizing Jn 6,7 with the other evangelists; while according to him only Philip speaks, according to Me 6,37 those present respond; Given this, it is reasonable to think that they could put pluralem numerumpro singulari. The same is said of Jn 6,9 with respect to Mt 14,17, Mark 6,38 and Luke 9, 13. In 2, 79, 156 regarding the comments made by the disciples on the pouring out of the costly perfume: While Mt 26, 8-9 and Mark 14,4-5 are put in the mouths of the disciples in general, John 12,4-5 attributes it only to John plurali number pro singulari usurpato. In 3,6,25 regarding Peter's denial; According to Mt 26:53 and Mark 14:70, it was all those present who questioned Peter, while according to Luke 22:59 and Jn 18:26 it was only one. The harmonization is established by Augustine arguing that Matthew and Mark used pluralem numerum pro singulari. Here that solution appears as an alternative to another: they put a compendium numerum pluralem. The divergences between Mt 27, 44 and Mark 15, 32, on the one hand, and Luke 23, 39, on the other, regarding the words of the two thieves crucified with Jesus, are resolved by Augustine considering that Matthew and Mark used pluralem numerumpro singulari, and he stops to explain how this interpretation fits without doing violence to the text (3, 16, 53). The same solution contributes to the divergences regarding the words of the soldiers, once Jesus was crucified (3, 17, 54). Finally, antonomasia, a kind of synecdoche. It is useful to bring here a text from the Quaestiones in Heptateuchum, a more erudite work where there is less hesitation in using the appropriate terms.

In response to one of the questions he explicitly formulates what is usual praxis in the work at hand: »There is no easier solution to this question than to resort to synecdoche••. Figure that explains, applied to the specific case, in the following way: "When in a whole a part is larger or more important (potior), what does not belong to the name itself is also usually designated by its name." And he gives an example: -For example, the case of Judas, who no longer belonged to the group of the twelve apostles... and, nevertheless, the apostle maintains the number of twelve in his letter when he says that the Lord appeared to the twelve- (1, 117: CSEL 28 / 2, 59). Although in reality there were no longer twelve, the number signified par excellence the group of apostles. In De consensu, however, the number that Augustine recognizes as used par excellence to designate the apostles is -eleven-. When he comes across the text of Luke "he appeared to the eleven and to those who were with them" (Luke 24, 33), he tries to decipher who those eleven are and discovers that they are the apostles: - Well, by adding And those who were with them, he sufficiently stated that they were called in a more eminent way (eminentius) "the eleven", with
Additional notes

who were the others, and from that it is understood that those were the apostles" (3, 25, 81; cf. also 3, 25, 76). Previously, referring to the appearances of the Lord, Augustine wrote: "According to John's account, it was Mary Magdalene, undoubtedly in the company of other women who had served the Lord, but she was much more fervent in her love, to the point that John mentions only her, silencing those who went with her, as the others testify (3, 24, 69). In these words, Augustine indicates that John resorted to synecdoche, the pane for the whole, Mary for all the others, specifically the antonomasia, the pars potior, in this case dilectioneferventior. The same resource serves to offer a possible solution to the divergences between Mt 9,1 (Jesus came to his own city) and Mark 2,1 (Jesus entered Capernaum). He comments: "Thus he rightly said that he had arrived at his city when he arrived in Galilee, regardless of the town in which he found himself, especially taking into account that Capernaum itself stood out (excellebat; shortly afterwards he will say eminebat) in Galilee, which was considered the metropolis." Augustine's argument has two stages: first he expands Jesus' concept of city to think not of Nazareth, but of Galilee; Then he considers that Mark resorted to synecdoche, he took the part for the whole, Capernaum for Galilee, specifically the antonomasia, since he chose Capernaum because it stood out {excellebat, eminebat) (2, 25, 58). Shortly before he had offered the same solution to the divergence between Mt 8:28, on the one hand, and Mark 5:1 and Luke 8:26, on the other. If the latter mention only one of the two (according to Matthew) swineherds possessed by the devil, it is because they wanted to signify that one belonged to someone, clarioris et famosioris (2,24,56). In short, Augustine found in synecdoche, in the variety of its presentations, an easy way to provide his harmonizing solution to many divergences among the evangelists. [28] «Locutiofigurata». The entire Augustinian work moves in a "literal" tone that never ceases to surprise, accustomed as Augustine's reader is to his recourse to the figurative sense in his dealings with Scripture. Augustine seeks harmony between the gospels from the proper meaning of the words. The statement is valid as long as it is not understood as totally excluding me from the other option, that of the figurative sense.

It must be recognized, in fact, that, although on rare occasions, Augustine resorts to it. And it must even be recognized that this resource is imposed by the pre-judgment of the truth of the Gospel stories, given that in some cases only in this way can the harmony between them be shown (3,25,80). That a term can have a variety of meanings is a principle with which the speaker and the writer play and which the literary critic must not forget. Many of the figures of speech and thought rely on it. Figures per inmutationem, at the service of ornamentation or clarity, need to be perceived to understand the meaning of a spoken or written text. There is a use of language in its own sense (proprie, ad litteram) and another in a figurative sense (figúrate), which is given by the author and which the interpreter must capture. This fact is explained by Augustine in a simple way to his readers: «There are many... words that do not have a single meaning, but, placed in a coherent way,

In fact, in the different passages they must be understood in different ways, and sometimes they appear already with the accompanying explanation (2, 30, 72; 3, 25, 80). Augustine is not speaking in theory, but referring specifically to Scripture. Not only the evangelist uses this double form of expression; also the Lord himself did it. Reality is frequent in Scripture and Augustine gives as examples the terms tentatio, puer, sapiens, onus (2, 30. 71. 72). This double level of language is designated by Augustine on one occasion with the terms spiritualiter and corporaliter. Spiritual understanding, in turn, usually also designates it with the term mystica significatio (2, 30, 75; 2, 75, 145) or figurata significatio (2, 30, 72; 3, 25, 80), which can be multiple (2, 30, 72). Another way of expressing it is to indicate the existence of a mystery, mysterii gratia (3,25,86). The confirmation of this literary reality allows him to harmonize more than one case of divergence between evangelists. It must be said that he does not abuse the principle and resorts to it only when the prejudice of the truth forces him to do so. Ordinarily, as we already pointed out, it prefers harmonization from the proper meaning of the terms. We indicated that both the evangelists and the Lord used figurative language; both in words and in thought. As for words, the evangelist Matthew (28, 1) uses -evening" with the meaning of "night", in a kind of synecdoche (3, 24, 65; cf. supplementary note 27: Synecdoche). Regarding thought, it is evident for Augustine in the use of the number of genealogies. With the number 40 of generations that he points out, Matthew wanted to signify, in accordance with his presentation of the royal function of Christ, the time in which it is appropriate for Christ to govern us in this world and on this earth (2, 4, 8); Likewise, the very structure of the genealogy, which in Jeconiah forms a kind of angle, is figurative language (praefigurabat) to indicate that Christ had to go from circumcision to the foreskin (2, 4, 10).

Also the number 77 of Luke is also a figurative language (significatur) to indicate the forgiveness of all sins (2, 4, 12-13). Mt 27,9-10, in turn, has been introduced on his own initiative by the evangelist elegantor et mystice, which in this case consists of his reference to the price paid by Christ (3, 7, 31). Applied to the words of the Lord, Augustine uses the resource non-uniformly. The possibilities that Augustine contemplates are these: Referring to a specific term: a) This is used in two sentences with different meanings: one proper and another figurative, and one evangelist picks up one sentence and another another. Referring to one or more sentences. b) The Lord has spoken in a proper sense and in a figurative sense and one evangelist has recorded the first and another the second, c) The Lord has spoken in figurative language and one evangelist has expressed it in one way and another in another, but coinciding. a) In one case he argues stating that a single term is used in a double meaning by the Lord; which has used both the proper meaning and a figurative one, according to a not uncommon practice. Without the possibility of a doubt it is noted in Mt 6:3, and not recognizing it is a sign of audacity and ignorance (2:30, 76). He resorts to this criterion to harmonize Mt 10,10 and Le 9,3 with Mark 6,8-9 - Excluding the possibility that they are sentences pronounced in different contexts,

There is no other way of solution than to admit that the Lord used the term virga with a double meaning (sub alia significatione). The difficulty is obviated by affirming that the Lord said one thing and another, but partim proprie, partim figúrate (2, 30, 71. 74-76). The objection arises from the fact that no evangelist collected the two sentences of the Lord; Had he done so, it would have been easier to understand that it was a double meaning given the improbability of him having contradicted himself so openly. The same solution must be applied regarding what was said in the same passages about footwear and tunics (2, 30, 76). b) In other cases it is not a question of a term being used in a double meaning, but rather of sentences pronounced in a figurative sense. This is what Augustine perceives regarding Luke 13:32. In this text, since it would contradict what actually happened, there is only room for figurative interpretation (mystice ab illo et figúrate dicta intelleguntur) (2, 75, 145). Said text, having no parallels, does not create a problem of harmonization; but it serves Augustine to deduce the need to also understand Lk 13, 35 in a figurative sense, in apparent contradiction with Mt 21,9 (cogit... etiam illud mystice intellegi). In the circumstance, Luke abandons the proper meaning (entry of Jesus into Jerusalem) in which Matthew expresses himself, to refer to the second coming of the Lord (2,75,145). The same procedure serves to harmonize Mt 24, 20 and Mark 13,18 with Le 21, 34-36. Here, unlike before, it is Luke who expresses in his own language what Matthew and Mark had indicated with figurative language, and in this sense he serves, as is his custom, for clarity (inlustrasse sententiam). Matthew's term sabbatum is used figuratively, as a signifier (significatum) of the debauchery that Luke's words prohibit (2, 77, 151). c) In another case, we find that harmonization comes through the figurative sense, but from both divergent texts; in this case Mt 24, 17 and Mark 13,15, on the one hand, and Le 21, 21 b, on the other. Without formulations of principle, Augustine affirms that in the variety of verbal expressions they said the same thing, with the particularity that none of them spoke in the proper sense, but all in the figurative sense, a term that Augustine does not mention here, and it is in him where the coincidence occurs.

The situation of the person with respect to the surrounded city indicates the attitude of the soul towards this earthly life (2, 77, 150). In this section we can also include the mutatio verbi that regarding Mt 24, 15 provides Mark 13,14, which is nothing more than a periphrasis that serves the clarity (exposuit) of the sententia (2, 77, 149). It is nothing more than what Augustine also defines the alia pro alus quae tamen idem valeant (2, 12, 28). If we look at the res expressed in the locutio figurata we perceive realities of moral content (2, 77, 150. 151), prophetic (3, 25, 86) or Christological (2, 77, 150, 151). 4, 8. 10; 2, 75, 145).
